#3264. Galantas CEO Mario Stifano on AI, data centres and the copper supply gap

Galantas CEO Mario Stifano explains why AI data centres depend on copper, power and new mines. Gold’s role in chips will grow, he says, but stay specialised.

Mario Stifano is chief executive of Galantas Gold, a gold and copper company listed on the TSX Venture Exchange in Toronto and on AIM in London. He has more than 25 years of experience across exploration, development and producing mining companies. Galantas is developing the Andacollo gold project in Chile, a former producing mine, and the Indiana gold-copper project.

We asked him how the AI and data-centre build-out is changing demand for gold, copper and new mines.

Gold has traditionally been viewed as a store of value, but it also plays an important role in advanced electronics and computing. As AI and digital infrastructure continue to expand, how do you see gold’s role in the technology sector evolving?

Most people picture gold in a vault or in jewellery. Fewer think about the gold inside the devices they use every day. Engineers have relied on it for decades because it conducts electricity well, doesn’t corrode, and can be made into extremely thin wires and coatings. When a connection has to work every time, those properties matter.

I expect that role to continue as computing becomes more demanding. But I wouldn’t assume every increase in AI investment means the same increase in gold demand. Manufacturers are always looking for ways to use less of an expensive material.

You can see that tug-of-war in the numbers. The World Gold Council reported about 323 tonnes of technology demand in 2025, essentially flat on 2024. AI applications supported demand, but thinner wires, leaner designs and weaker consumer electronics offset that growth. So gold can become more important in specific high-end components without a dramatic jump in total tonnage.

The rapid expansion of AI data centers is driving demand for copper and other essential materials. How is this infrastructure boom reshaping demand for metals, and where does gold fit into the broader picture?

Start with the electricity. A data centre needs reliable power every hour it operates. That means looking past the servers to the substations, cables, transformers and generating capacity behind them.

The IEA’s latest analysis found that data-centre electricity use grew 17% in 2025. It expects that use to roughly double by 2030, with AI-focused facilities growing faster still. That gives you a sense of the physical build-out that companies are planning.

Copper runs through that whole electrical system. And AI is adding demand at the same time as utilities, transport and industry are investing in electrification. The mining industry has to plan for all of it together.

Gold plays a different role. It’s used selectively in electronics, where reliability justifies the cost, while copper’s exposure is spread across the physical infrastructure. For gold, technology matters, but it is still one part of a market driven mainly by investment, central banks and jewellery.

As tech companies invest billions in AI infrastructure, could growing demand for copper and other critical materials create supply chain bottlenecks that ultimately slow down technological progress?

Yes. The technology industry and the mining industry work on very different timelines. A commitment to spend billions on AI infrastructure doesn’t mean the materials will be there when construction teams need them.

S&P Global found that mines starting production between 2020 and 2024 took almost 18 years on average from discovery. Before construction even begins, a company has to drill the deposit, prove its economics, complete engineering, obtain approvals and secure financing.

For copper, the pressure goes well beyond AI. Data centres compete for supply with electricity networks, electric vehicles and other industries. The IEA’s 2026 outlook estimates that, under today’s policies, existing and announced projects could leave primary copper supply about 25% short of requirements in 2035.

Closing that gap takes more than new discoveries. It means financing projects that can actually deliver, expanding and restarting suitable operations, and recovering more from ore already being processed. Otherwise, technology companies face higher costs, longer equipment lead times and delayed projects.

That’s why I put so much weight on work that has already been done. Our Andacollo gold project in Chile is a former producing mine. We still have refurbishment, technical and financing work ahead of us, but we’re not starting from a blank page.

AI is increasingly being used to analyze geological data and identify mineral deposits. How could these technologies transform gold exploration, particularly when it comes to discovering resources that traditional methods may have overlooked?

One opportunity that really interests me is getting more out of work that has already been done.

An established mining district can hold decades of drilling, surveys and geological records. Different companies collected that information at different times, often looking for different things. There’s real value in bringing it together and asking questions that were hard to investigate before.

Canada is backing exactly this idea, with a federal and territorial pilot in the Northwest Territories that uses AI to scan and analyse drill core already sitting in government storage.

The majors are doing it too. Agnico Eagle works with GeologicAI, combining AI with drill-core scanning to make its resource models more complete and reliable.

At Galantas, our team in Chile spends a lot of time reading drill core and surface geology, and we share some of that work through our Field Notes video series. Technology can help, but experienced geologists still have to understand the core.

And you still have to drill. A model can suggest where to look; it can’t prove you have an economic deposit. For me the test is simple: does it help the team make a better decision about the next drill hole? Exploration capital is limited, so better targeting makes a real difference to how far that capital goes.

Gold is valued in high-reliability electronic components for its conductivity and resistance to corrosion. Could advances in AI hardware, semiconductors, and high-performance computing create new opportunities for gold, or will its role remain relatively specialized?

Specialised doesn’t mean unimportant. A component can contain very little gold and still depend on it to perform reliably.

There are new applications worth watching. One is co-packaged optics, which places optical connections right next to the processor so AI systems can move data faster and use less power. Some of the optical components and high-frequency electrodes in those designs use gold.

The World Gold Council sees it as a potentially small but meaningful new source of demand if it’s widely adopted in AI data centres. It’s still early.

I’d leave the engineering judgments to the chip makers. From a mining perspective, I want to know three things. Is the technology being adopted commercially? How much material does it need? And can something cheaper do the same job?

There will always be pressure to use less gold because of its price. But where it offers a clear reliability advantage, it earns its place. That points to a specialised role with room to grow, not a story where AI suddenly transforms the whole gold market.

Building the next generation of AI data centers requires massive investments in electricity grids and power distribution systems, where copper plays a critical role. Are technology companies underestimating their dependence on physical resources, and what happens if supply cannot keep pace?

I wouldn’t assume the technology companies don’t understand the dependency. The better question is whether everyone in the chain is working to a realistic timetable.

A server can be ordered. A grid connection may need new lines, approvals and equipment that can’t be delivered right away. The IEA has estimated that, unless these constraints are addressed, around 20% of planned data-centre projects worldwide could be at risk of delay. That’s mainly a grid problem rather than a copper shortage, but it shows how physical the AI build-out really is.

The supply chain also runs deeper than most people realise. In its 2026 outlook, the IEA warned that the near-term copper supply picture has worsened considerably, partly because of tight supplies of sulphuric acid. Many copper operations need that reagent to process their ore, and Chile, where we operate, is one of the major producers that use the process. Most people in tech have never thought about sulphuric acid, but it can affect how much copper reaches the market.

If supply can’t keep pace, companies will delay projects, pay more or build somewhere else. Long-term purchasing commitments and earlier conversations with suppliers help those suppliers expand with confidence. In mining, we know a good asset is only part of the equation; you also need power, infrastructure and financing. Digital infrastructure is no different.

How are machine learning, automation, and predictive analytics changing the economics of gold exploration and production, and could these technologies help smaller companies compete more effectively with established industry players?

The biggest opportunity is getting more value from the money we already spend. Drilling is expensive. Equipment downtime is expensive. Losing recoverable gold during processing is expensive. Those are specific problems technology can help address.

In exploration, better analysis of historical drilling and geological information can help a team decide where to drill next. It doesn’t guarantee a discovery, but better targeting can help a company make more effective use of its exploration budget.

In production, consider recovery: the percentage of metal in the ore that the plant successfully extracts. In a simplified example, if the material processed contains 100,000 ounces of gold, improving recovery from 90% to 92% means recovering another 2,000 ounces from the same feed. You still have to account for the cost of achieving that improvement, but you haven’t had to mine additional tonnes to access those ounces.

There are practical examples of this approach. BHP and Microsoft have described using real-time plant data and AI recommendations at Escondida to help operators adjust processing conditions with the aim of improving copper recovery.

Predictive maintenance tackles another cost. Identifying a developing equipment problem can allow a repair during a planned shutdown instead of an unexpected failure that interrupts production.

For smaller companies, access to specialist software and service providers can put better analytical tools within reach. But the tools still need reliable data and experienced people. Large operators retain advantages in both.

I would start with a problem we can measure, test the technology and compare the benefit with its full cost. A smaller company doesn’t need to match a major miner’s technology budget. It needs to spend its own budget effectively.

As the technology industry looks for more sustainable supply chains, could advances in electronic waste recycling, AI-driven material recovery, and more efficient production reduce the need for newly mined gold and copper?

Yes, to a degree. Recovering more metal from products we’ve already made makes sense. The question is how much can be collected and recovered economically, and when it becomes available.

The UN’s Global E-waste Monitor found that only 22.3% of the e-waste generated in 2022 was documented as formally collected and recycled. That’s measured by weight, not the recovery rate for any one metal, but it shows how much room there is to improve.

AI-assisted sorting and better processing can help. They still need collection networks, suitable facilities and a business model that covers the cost.

Timing matters too. Recycling depends on products reaching the end of their lives, and copper installed in a grid today may stay in service for decades.

So I see recycling and mining as complementary. More recycling improves supply security and reduces how many new mines we need. It doesn’t remove the need to invest in mining.

Looking toward 2030, which developments do you believe will have the greatest impact on the future of gold and critical metals: AI-powered exploration, rising demand from data centers, or the challenge of bringing new mineral supplies online?

For the period to 2030, I’d put delivering supply first. I also think it’s the one the market gives the least weight.

A discovery made today might be very important, but it’s unlikely to produce metal before 2030. That makes the projects already being permitted, financed and built far more relevant this decade. So is what existing operations can add through expansions, better recovery and sensible restarts.

AI will help with those decisions. I expect much of its near-term value to come from understanding known assets better and helping operations run more consistently.

But the asset still has to work. It needs the right geology and metallurgy, a realistic development plan, financing and the ability to operate responsibly. Better software doesn’t change that.

I’d also separate gold from copper. Data centres are part of copper’s wider infrastructure story. For gold, technology plays a role, but monetary conditions, investment demand and central-bank buying will matter more.

The question I keep coming back to is simple: which projects can actually deliver, at what cost, and when?

The Saucony Endorphin Speed has been one of the best running shoes on the market ever since the original launched in 2020.

It’s always been one of the most versatile shoes available thanks to its fast, comfortable ride, and I loved the Saucony Endorphin Speed 5 when I racked up over 60 miles in it for my four-star review.

The new Endorphin Speed 6 just launched, and that’s resulted in some great deals cropping up on the Endorphin Speed 5, which is $129 in the Amazon sale right now.

The Endorphin Speed 5 is a super-trainer with a nylon plate and a comfortable but quick ride that makes it ideal for all kinds of daily training runs. Most colors and sizes of the shoe are reduced on Amazon right now, making it a better value buy than the new Endorphin Speed 6 in my opinion.

For me that discount makes it the better buy ahead of the new shoe, because although Saucony has made some changes to the Endorphin Speed 6, the overall ride feel is still similar based on my early testing.

The main change made to the Endorphin Speed 6 is that it uses a new midsole foam called PWRRUN PBX, which is meant to be a little lighter and softer than the PWRRUN PB foam on the Endorphin Speed 5.

Saucony also slightly increased the midsole stack height in the new shoe by 2mm, so it is a little more cushioned all round than the Endorphin Speed 5, while also making minor updates to the upper and outsole, and adjusting the shape of the nylon plate in the midsole.

On paper the updates sound significant with the new shoe, but when I did my first run in the Endorphin Speed 6 it certainly felt very familiar.

The midsole foam is a little softer, but still quite firm, and the Speedroll rocker on the shoe pushes you smoothly onto your forefoot at both easy and faster paces.

I very much enjoyed the run in the Speed 6, but I was surprised how similar to the Speed 5 it felt, so I actually ran in both shoes at the same time to compare them directly.

There are slight differences – the new shoe is marginally softer at the heel in particular — but overall I do think they have a similar ride feel.

While the Speed 6 might be a slight upgrade overall, I’d certainly be happy grabbing the older shoe in the sale for $50 less, since the Endorphin Speed 6 will set you back $180 right now.

Following last week’s release of macOS 27.2, Apple has now kicked off the next round of beta testing with the first developer beta of macOS 27.3 Golden Gate. Here are the details.

It’s been an unusually eventful few weeks for Mac users. In addition to several security releases for macOS Tahoe 26.7.2 and macOS Sequoia 15.8.2, Apple released macOS 27.2 Golden Gate lats week, with expanded language support for Siri AI and new conversation recall capabilities.

On the hardware side, Apple recently announced new M6-powered iMacs and 14-inch MacBook Pro, and the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display “with Touch,” as Apple has been addressing it.

Now, Apple is rolling out the first developer beta of macOS 27.3 Golden Gate, which will possibly include support for additional Siri AI languages, including Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese, as Apple has promised to expand availability by the end of the year.

macOS 27.3 also brings several new features to Safari, including Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and the ability to organize tabs using Siri AI. You can read more about those changes here.

The update also comes as Apple prepares to launch Apple Intelligence in China with iOS 27.3. However, the company has confirmed that the initial rollout will be exclusive to the iPhone, with support for other platforms coming only after the necessary regulatory approvals have been obtained.

macOS 27.3 may also most likely include further under-the-hood refinements to the macOS interface to accommodate touchscreen input, building on the new gesture recognition tools introduced in macOS 27.2.

#3261. Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler Is 2027 IEEE President-Elect

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

He has been an active volunteer for more than 30 years

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler is the 2027 IEEE president-elect.

IEEE Life Fellow Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler has been elected as the 2027 IEEE president-elect. He will begin serving as president on 1 January 2028.

Schindler, who was nominated by the IEEE Board of Directors, received 16,421 votes in the election. Senior Member David Alan Koehler received 13,874 votes.

Schindler’s Top 3 Goals as President-Elect Strengthen IEEE’s connection with industry by coordinating events across geography, industry, and technology to revitalize professional activities, especially ones for young professionals.Champion the improvement of IEEE’s digital infrastructure to eliminate manual processes and modernize interfaces.Prioritize the advancement of technology to benefit future generations by expanding and supporting IEEE initiatives and programs.

At press time, the results were unofficial until the IEEE Board of Directors accepts the IEEE Teller’s Committee report in November.

Schindler, an expert in microwave semiconductor technology, is an independent consultant supporting clients with technical expertise, due diligence, and project management.

Throughout his career, he led the development of microwave integrated-circuit technology, from lab demonstrations to high-volume commercial products. He has numerous technical publications and holds 11 patents.

Schindler served as CTO of Anlotek, and director of Qorvo and RFMD’s Boston design center. He was applications manager at IBM, engineering manager at ATN Microwave, and a lab manager at Raytheon.

An IEEE volunteer for more than 30 years, Schindler served as the 2024 vice president of IEEE Technical Activities and the 2021–2022 Division IV director. He was chair of the IEEE Conferences Committee from 2015 to 2018 and president of the IEEE Microwave Theory and Technology Society (MTTS) in 2003. He received the society’s 2018 Distinguished Service Award and its 2015 N. Walter Cox Award. His award-winning micro-business column has appeared in IEEE Microwave Magazine since 2011.

He also led the 2025 One IEEE to Enable Strategic Investments in Innovations and Public Imperative Activities adhoc committee.

Schindler is an IEEE–Eta Kappa Nu member and a MTTS honorary life member.

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute, covering the work and accomplishments of IEEE members and IEEE and technology-related events. She has a master's degree in health communications from Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, N.J.

#3259. Intrepid Potash (IPI) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Trio output climbed 19% as Moab harvest timing shifted.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Intrepid Potash, Inc. (IPI +1.72%) reported its third quarter results, highlighting a strategy focused on operational execution and capital discipline. Management reported increased Trio production and improved segment gross margins despite seasonal weakness and a strategic delay in the potash harvest season. The company stated that it is prioritizing organic growth through investments in its existing assets while returning capital to shareholders through share repurchases. Additionally, the company noted that selection for federal matching funding for a new sulfate of potash facility represents a potential expansion into specialty fertilizer markets.

Operator: Thank you for standing by. This is the conference moderator. Welcome to the Intrepid Potash Q3 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] The conference is being recorded. [Operator Instructions] I would now like to turn the conference over to Ryan Schultz, Investor Relations Manager. Please go ahead.

Ryan Schultz: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us to discuss Intrepid's third quarter 2026 results. With me today are Kevin Crutchfield, our Chief Executive Officer; Zach Adams, our Vice President of Sales and Marketing; Rick Kim, our Vice President of Operations; and Jason Tremblay, our Chief Financial Officer. Before I turn the call over to Kevin, I want to remind everyone that today's discussion contains forward-looking statements about future business and financial expectations. The Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 provides a safe harbor from civil litigation for such forward-looking statements.

Actual results may differ significantly from those projected in today's forward-looking statements due to various risks and uncertainties, including the risks described in our periodic reports filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Except as required by law, we undertake no obligation to update our forward-looking statements. Further, this call will include the discussion of certain non-GAAP financial measures. Reconciliation of these measures to the closest GAAP financial measure is included in our earnings press release and corresponding SEC filings, which are available at intrepidpotash.com. With that, I'll turn the call over to Kevin.

Kevin Crutchfield: Thank you, Ryan, and good morning, everyone. On last quarter's call, I discussed the 3 pillars of our own value creation strategy: execution, opportunity, and capital discipline. We made good progress on all 3 of these fronts during the third quarter. With respect to our execution, we increased production in Trio during the third quarter. This operating performance supports a 10,000 ton increase in our full year 2026 Trio production guidance and positions us to target annual production of more than 300,000 tons, a goal we didn't expect to achieve until sometime in 2027. We're acutely focused on the reliability and predictability of our operations, and we're pleased with the improving track record that we're establishing.

Rick will discuss the operating drivers behind this progress shortly. With respect to opportunity as the only U.S.-based producer of muriate of potash and 1 of only 2 global producers of langbeinite, the mineral we market as Trio, we see significant potential to unlock value through organic growth investment. In potash, our opportunity lies in our ability to increase production while moving down the cost curve through operational excellence. We expect to lower production costs, and combined with our transportation cost advantage in our core markets and the diversity of our offerings, we expect to drive profitable growth in our potash business. Trio's combination of low chloride potassium, magnesium, and sulfate gives us a differentiated platform for growth.

We believe that potential growth in demand for sulfur nutrition could support this opportunity over time. Zach will discuss the market backdrop for the products in more detail shortly. We believe consistent execution, rigorous cost controls, and strategic organic growth investments can unlock the earnings potential of our existing assets, driving profitability and improved free cash flow conversion. While cyclical, the domestic market for agricultural nutrient is large, and third-party industry forecasts generally anticipate growth over the coming years. Importantly, as we've seen in recent years, the fertilizer market is highly sensitive to global geopolitical disruptions and thus, a matter of national security.

As such, Intrepid is a well-positioned domestic critical mineral producer with attractive production assets in close proximity to key U.S. growing regions. Against this backdrop, as we announced on October 26, the USDA selected our proposed sulfate of potash, or SOP, project near Carlsbad, New Mexico, for approximately $139 million and proposed matching funding through its FIELDS program. Based on current project plans, the facility would have annual production capacity of approximately 220,000 tons. If constructed, it would introduce a new product to our portfolio, complementing Trio and potash and expanding our presence in specialty fertilizer markets. This could be a pivotal project for Intrepid, allowing us to turn American minerals into a fertilizer product American farmers need.

The project is in the advanced stages of planning and evaluation but remain subject to completion of the award process, fulfillment of all applicable grant conditions, and a final investment decision, which we're currently targeting for late 2027. As we continue our evaluation, we remain focused on disciplined capital deployment and generating attractive long-term returns on invested capital. We look forward to sharing additional details as the project advances. Our operational improvements and the constructive selling price environment contributed to the solid cash flow we generated through the first 9 months of this year.

The cash flow, combined with the proceeds from the sale of our South Ranch asset in the second quarter, puts us in a financial position that gives us multiple pathways to shareholder value creation. Jason will review our capital allocation framework in more detail shortly, but I want to outline our two-pronged returns-focused strategy for deploying capital. First, we've identified several attractive organic growth opportunities within our existing asset base. We're in the final stages of evaluating capital investments designed to increase production volumes and lower unit costs across both segments. Jason will discuss the 2 principal projects we plan to pursue in 2027.

We believe these investments can generate attractive returns and support sustained growth over the next several years. Also on the organic growth front, our development partners continue to advance the Wendover Lithium project as they work to complete their definitive feasibility study. Discussions with potential off-takers are also in the advanced stages. In addition to growth investments, we're returning capital to shareholders through share repurchases. During the quarter, we repurchased shares under our $50 million share repurchase authorization. We would plan to accelerate the utilization of this program depending on how far below intrinsic value we believe our shares are trading.

While we purchased a limited number of shares in the third quarter, over the past 5 weeks, we've accelerated our repurchasing activity, bringing the total shares we bought since the end of June to approximately 88,000. Share repurchases are a core component of our returns-focused approach to capital allocation, not a residual use of cash. We'll continue to weigh every dollar of capital, whether directed to share repurchases, improvements to our existing operations, or potential new growth projects, against the returns it can generate for shareholders, with a clear priority on compounding per share value over time.

Before I turn it over to Zach, I'd like to extend a special thanks to all of our employees for the work they've led over the last couple of years. By working together, we've increased our production in both Trio and potash. We substantially reduced our cost in Trio and are working similarly on our potash cost structure. As a result of their good work, our assets are performing much better, more predictably and reliably as demonstrated by increasing levels of profitability over the last several quarters. I'll close by noting the 3 pillars I outlined earlier, execution, opportunity, and capital discipline are converging into a cohesive value creation framework for Intrepid.

We're making good progress formulating that framework, and we see an opportunity to generate significant returns on invested capital through organic growth investment, share repurchases, and operational execution. As that work matures, we look forward to sharing more detail with you over the coming quarters. Now I'll turn the call over to Zach for a closer look at demand, pricing and the market outlook for potash and Trio.

Looking ahead, we are monitoring factors that could tighten the supply/demand balance in early 2027. In particular, congestion at Baltic ports is currently constraining exports from Russia and Belarus. If these shipping constraints persist into next year, they could limit available supply and provide further support for the market. We are also monitoring reports that negotiations have started on the next annual potash contract in China, where another early settlement could support continued shipment activity and help keep global supply and demand balances tight. Global sulfur supply constraints are contributing to higher input costs for some sulfate of potash producers, putting pressure on operating rates and availability. A tighter market for low-chloride potassium fertilizers could support demand for Trio.

With sulfur constraints extending beyond sulfate of potash to other sulfur-containing fertilizers, Trio's sulfate sulfur component provides an attractive value proposition for growers heading into spring. Trio is a unique product that supplies 3 essential plant nutrients, low-chloride potassium, magnesium, and sulfate in a naturally occurring mineral. Current supply conditions could enhance the appeal of that combination. Importantly, the sulfur in Trio occurs naturally within the langbeinite mineral we mine and is immediately available to the plants in the sulfate form. We do not need to purchase sulfur feedstock to produce Trio, reducing our exposure to the feedstock constraints affecting some other fertilizer producers.

We believe this positions Trio well to serve growers seeking low chloride potassium, magnesium, and sulfur nutrition. Looking ahead to spring 2027, grower sentiment has improved although elevated input costs continue to encourage disciplined purchase decisions. Demand will be subject to regional and seasonal variation but we believe growers remain focused on maximizing yields and making effective nutrient investments. Against that backdrop, we expect continued healthy fertilizer demand through the first half of 2027. With that market context, I'll turn the call over to Rick to discuss our operating performance and the initiatives supporting our increased production outlook.

Richard Kim: Thanks, Zach. I'll focus on the operating improvements behind our third quarter production gains and the work underway to improve reliability, efficiency, and unit costs across our operations. At our potash operations, we are focused on continuing to increase production while maintaining spending discipline. On a year-to-date basis, we have held total spending approximately flat while increasing output allowing us to spread fixed costs across more tons resulting in lower unit production costs. In our HB Mine, improvements in pond management and mill recovery have contributed to increases in production volume. These changes are helping us recover additional product that otherwise would have been lost as waste.

We deliberately delayed the start of the harvest season at Moab to allow additional evaporation in our ponds. After evaluating several operating scenarios, we determined that this timing would better support long-term production by adding more tons of inventory. While this decision reduced third quarter production, we expect to recover those tons by year-end. We also expect the additional evaporation to support higher production at Moab in 2027 and a corresponding reduction in unit costs. Decisions like this reflect our focus on optimizing performance across our operations. Turning to our Trio segment. Production increased 19% year-over-year during the third quarter, driven largely by continued improvements in operating performance at the East mine.

Our team is increasing equipment availability, reducing downtime and improving productivity. Year-over-year, operating hours increased by 5%, while tons per operating hour increased by approximately 20%. We believe these improvements provide a sustainable foundation for further production growth. Higher production improved operating leverage and contributed to a 13% year-over-year reduction in cost of goods sold per ton. Together with higher realized selling prices, these improvements supported stronger segment gross margin. As Kevin noted, we are increasing our full year 2026 Trio production guidance by 10,000 tons. Our focus is on sustaining these gains while continuing to improve reliability, productivity, and unit costs. With that, I'll turn the call over to Jason to review our third quarter financial results and outlook.

Jason Tremblay: Thank you, Rick. Third quarter sales from continuing operations were roughly flat with the prior year quarter at $51 million. Gross margin from continuing operations was also in line with last year's third quarter at $10 million. Net income from continuing operations improved to $1.7 million or $0.13 per diluted share from $700,000 or $0.05 per diluted share last year. Adjusted EBITDA from continuing operations increased to $11.7 million from $10.7 million last year. As a reminder, the third quarter is typically 1 of our seasonally weakest quarters, given that it follows the spring planting season and precedes the fall fertilizer application season. In the Trio segment, sales increased to $19.1 million from $18.1 million in the prior year quarter.

Sales volumes were flat, while average net realized selling price increased 1.5%. Most notably, Trio gross margin increased 33% year-over-year, driven by the positive impact of a 13,000 ton increase in production volume, which improved absorption and reduced Trio's cost of goods sold per ton, as well as favorable product mix. In Potash, segment sales were $31.3 million compared with $32.5 million in the prior year quarter. Sales volumes declined to 59,000 tons from 62,000 tons, while average net realized sales price increased 3.4% to $394 per ton. Production volume declined 17%. As Rick discussed earlier, we made a strategic decision to delay the start-up of our Moab facility following the summer evaporation process to support production levels and efficiency.

Potash segment gross margin declined due to higher COGS per ton, reflecting a production mix weighted more heavily toward Intrepid's higher cost sites as compared to last year's third quarter. Moving to cash flow and liquidity. Year-to-date cash flow from continuing operations was $50.5 million compared with $37.3 million in the prior year, with the increase partly attributable to improved operating performance. Capital spending remained disciplined with $11.3 million invested in the third quarter and $24.9 million year-to-date. We ended the third quarter with $152.3 million in cash and cash equivalents, $9.1 million in short-term investments and no debt.

As part of our capital allocation framework, we invested $14.5 million in short and long-term investments during the third quarter to earn additional returns on cash we've set aside to support our long-term balance sheet strength. Going forward, we'll continue to manage our liquidity carefully, balancing opportunities to earn returns on our cash with seasonal working capital needs investments in our growth projects and ongoing share repurchases. As Kevin mentioned, our balanced approach to capital allocation prioritizes a safe and reliable operations balance sheet flexibility and investments evaluated against the risk-adjusted return potential, execution readiness, and strategic fit. Within this framework, we will also return capital to shareholders.

As I discussed during last quarter's call, balance sheet preservation is the foundation of our capital allocation strategy. We plan to maintain approximately $50 million in liquidity to navigate cyclical downturns plus roughly $35 million for working capital needs and cash flow variability. Beyond these amounts, we will deploy capital through disciplined growth investments, particularly within our existing operating footprint and share repurchases. As Kevin indicated, we have increased our repurchase activity over the past several weeks. Since the Board approved the $50 million authorization in June, we repurchased 88,000 shares for a total of $3 million. Turning to growth investments.

Our planned spending in 2027 will focus on Trio production growth and potash mine development within our existing asset base. These investments are designed to increase production, extend the life of existing operations, and enhance the business' long-term earnings potential. The Trio and Potash investments I'll discuss are separate from the proposed SOP project, Kevin outlined. As we continue evaluating that opportunity ahead of a final investment decision, we remain committed to our broader capital allocation priorities and will assess the project within the same disciplined returns-focused framework. For Trio, we plan to invest approximately $16 million in 2027 as part of a broader initiative to increase annual production by approximately 30,000 tons above the first half 2026 run rates.

We expect this initiative to generate an internal rate of return of approximately 30%. We anticipate realizing some of the production benefits in late 2026 and expect full year 2027 Trio production in the range of 320,000 to 330,000 tons. We believe there is potential to increase annual Trio production by an additional 100,000 tons with modest incremental investment beyond 2027. For Potash, we plan to invest approximately $20 million in mine development in 2027 to sustain annual production at levels approximately 20,000 to 30,000 tons above prior years, with expected rates of return of approximately 30%. To support these initiatives, we are increasing our full year 2026 capital expenditure guidance to approximately $45 million from approximately $40 million previously.

In summary, we executed well during the third quarter, making meaningful progress toward our stated goals. We increased Trio production and significantly improved the segment's margins. Our strong balance sheet and disciplined capital allocation strategy position us to invest in organic growth while returning capital to shareholders through opportunistic share repurchases. Collectively, we expect these efforts to create long-term value for our shareholders. Operator, we are now ready to begin the Q&A.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from the line of Lucas Beaumont with UBS.

Lucas Beaumont: Just wanted to start on Trio. So I mean, pricing is up 25% or so over the last 2 years, I mean, probably half of that sort of came before the sort of more recent disruptions to the sulfur markets. So I just kind of wanted to get your view on, I guess, how would you sort of frame that in terms of what do you see as sort of temporary pricing uplift there versus what's been more structurally driven by the supply/demand setup.

So I guess as we sort of go forward and then see a normalization in those temporary factors, how much of that would you sort of expect to sort of roll off versus sort of being supported on an underlying basis?

Zachry Adams: Lucas, thank you for the question. In regards to Trio pricing and the changes we've seen over the last several years, we would assign that to a structural change. And yes, the global disruptions to sulfur are supporting that now, but on a broader level, there is just a greater awareness and recognition of magnesium and sulfur needs increasing over time in soil nutrient levels. And in combination with that as well is we're seeing a greater appreciation for the low-chloride content of Trio as well in specialty crop. So it's really all 3 components: the low-chloride potassium, the magnesium and the sulfur all having broader awareness and recognition that's helping to structurally change that price dynamic.

Kevin Crutchfield: The other thing I'd add too, Lucas, is given the conflict in the Mid East, I mean that's obviously provided some underfooting for higher sulfur prices. And to the extent that, that gets resolved tomorrow, it's not going to come back quickly. We don't think just based on the level of infrastructure damage that's been done across the system. So you can refer to it as temporary, if you want, but our view is that it's going to take a long time to get that anywhere back to normal.

Lucas Beaumont: Great. And then I guess just on the potash side, considering the markets that have been fairly balanced through the middle part of the year here, and you're kind of expecting pricing to sort of be flat to kind of slightly lower end of the fourth quarter sequentially. So I guess, how do you sort of see the set up there for market momentum for potash into the fall and then peak spring demand. I mean, you sort of see the market as tight enough that we should see pricing move higher into the spring? Or kind of what's your view currently?

Zachry Adams: Lucas, regarding the potash market, we see that as very constructive. To your point, it has been balanced throughout the year, but as we enter the fourth quarter here, there's several things going on globally. One is the reengagement of the Chinese on their next potash contract, which could drive kind of shipments to continue to be at very ratable heavy clip what we've done year-to-date. And the other more, I'd say, thing we're watching even closer is the disruption to the ports in the Baltic. Estimates are that could impact up to 1.5 million tons here in fourth quarter of potash from Russia and Belarus that would not be able to be exported.

And we kind of pair that with an improving grower sentiment and good demand on potash that we've seen this fall and we expect to continue into the spring season. There certainly is some factors that could lead to a tightening market as we get in the first quarter of next year.

Lucas Beaumont: And then I guess just on your production improvement initiatives there for next year, I mean, that's fairly substantial again as well. You're sort of pointing to another kind of 10% increase. So I was just wondering if you could give us a bit more detail there. I guess, on sort of what you're doing? And then what sort of a cash cost to production benefit should we, I guess, be thinking about with that kind of 10% uplift?

Kevin Crutchfield: Yes, Lucas. Good question. So on Potash and Trio, I mean the investments are different, obviously, I think on Trio, rather than talking about anything specifically we're going to do -- we just want to talk about the Trio product as a system from the mine face continuous miner shuttle cars, belt, plant infrastructure, yields, et cetera. We just -- we think there are opportunities to improve operating run time, maintenance downtime, mill throughput, yields, et cetera. And that monies -- those monies will go into just generally, I would describe as system improvements to generate better volumes over time. And it's not a sort of a onetime thing. We think that's a sustainable long-term run rate.

And we think there's upside potential beyond that which is premature to get into today. So that's kind of how we think about Trio. I'm not going to talk much more about what 1 miner does or whatever. We're just going to talk about it as improvements to the system and continuing to debottleneck the system to generate better production over time. And then on the Potash side, it's an investment that is developmental in nature to replace tons as they fall off over the future, but it will stimulate production 20,000 to 30,000 tons. We'll start to realize that next year. And look, I'd also point out, too, that some context here is important.

When we -- when you look at the numbers we've provided in terms of next year's range of guidance. You're in the mid 600,000 ton range. And it's been, I don't know, a decade or so since the company has achieved anywhere near that. And so I think that's an important part of the story that's not getting captured appropriately. And those gains have largely come over the last 2.5 or 3 years. And I'd like to credit the team that we have in place and the good work that's being done at the site level to generating those positive outcomes. I'll refer to Jason for any sort of remarks around the cost piece.

Jason Tremblay: Yes. So on the cost front. These are -- I would call them marginal tons, right? So I think what you get is much of your fixed cost isn't going to adjust. There's some amount of investment in fixed cost that come. Majority of this is marginal production with marginal costs being added. As a result, you see a pretty -- we're a high fixed cost business and you see that benefit come through. That answer is very specific to Trio and I'll get into the Potash side. But on the Trio side, you should see cost benefits just through absorption.

As we come to the Potash side, I think if you look at it on any individual mine, you're going to see cost benefits of these investments, right? So -- and largely, what this mine development does is provide higher grade to the facilities, which drives kind of more efficient production. Really, your costs aren't changing much. You're handling the same volume of raw materials to produce incremental volume. So you're getting better volume for largely similar cost structure at most of that -- at the sites.

The thing that gets hard is -- and Q3 is a good example of that, is depending which site we're producing tons at and where the relative cost positions are, you can get unusual movement in the consolidated result, right? And that's something we're going to expand on more as we move into the future and just help make sure that we help the investors and understand kind of the relative cost performance of site because I think that's a big driver that moves pieces around. But what we do know is each of our sites should see cost improvement as the mine development takes hold and the production improves.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line Vincent Andrews with Morgan Stanley.

Justin Pellegrino: This is Justin Pellegrino on for Vincent. My first question is about Trio production. And if you just annualize 2H '26 Trio production. It implies about 332,000 tons of production at today's rates which -- that's above the 2027 production guidance. So 2 questions there. Does the '27 production guidance includes some conservatism? Or do you guys expect current rates to kind of come down a little bit maybe? And then likewise, does the '27 production guidance include any additional tons from the $16 million that you plan to invest in '27?

Kevin Crutchfield: Yes, there's a lot in that question. So out of the $16 million that we called out, we're going to spend -- start spending a little bit of that this year. That's why we raised our capital guide a little bit. You're right, the run rate of late has been really solid but it's dangerous to annualize a quarter. So what we're trying to do is build sustainable run rates that are reliable, predictable, and dependable just like I've been saying for the last few years. So a piece of that is, is there upside in that?

Absolutely, because the team there is -- they've become very dedicated to thinking about the Trio production system as just that a system and just debottlenecking kind of weak point by weak point by weak point. And every time you do that, you generate better volumes over time. So we still think there's tremendous upside potential left on the Trio side. And we'll continue to update it on a quarterly basis. Anything you'd add?

Jason Tremblay: Yes. The only thing I'd add to that is just to your -- the first part of your answer when you were talking about -- it's dangerous to annualize a quarter. You have to keep in mind, right, there is scheduled downtime required for our assets for major maintenance. We have to take turnaround activities on specific assets and timing of those matter, right?

And so in the second half here, we're lighter on the maintenance front and lighter in terms of major asset maintenance, which is why you're seeing a higher run rate, but it's also indicative of the fact that we can run at higher rates but that's why I think you're seeing kind of a change in guide.

Justin Pellegrino: Understood, and that's much appreciated. And then the next -- I know this is kind of trying to isolate 2027 and investments happen at different points throughout the year. But if we simply just add the $16 million of Trio and $20 million that you called out in Potash to the $45 million of guidance, you get to somewhere in the $80 million ballpark of CapEx 2027. So I was just hoping you could maybe help us figure out if that's in the right ballpark. I know you had mentioned previously some maybe larger sustaining CapEx items as well in '27. So just any kind of help us triangulate where 2027 CapEx could land?

Kevin Crutchfield: Yes. I'll take the initial part of that, Jason, will probably have some color to add. But if you imputed that the way you just described, you'd be too high. So yes, we did this year from -- I mean, we started, I think, the year $45 million, we moved it down $40 million. We've moved it back up to $45 million because we wanted to get a head start on some of next year. So $5 million of that $36 million is happening this year. But the addition of those 2 numbers is not going to get you close to what we're talking about for sustaining. Next year, it will be south of that.

But we're not prepared to give full year guidance just yet. We'll do that next quarter.

Jason Tremblay: The only thing I'd add, Justin, to that, just context-wise, right, we do mine development activity every year, right? It's just given the magnitude of it that's falling next year, we wanted to provide some context to that and the return profile. And I would say the same thing on the Trio front. There's reliability type investments ongoing year-over-year. But again, we wanted to provide context because it will be a bit higher next year. So we just want to make sure people understand these are being done with a return focus, right? And -- but I agree wholeheartedly with Kevin's comment, which is why you just can't add the 2 numbers together.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Jason Ursaner with Bumbershoot Holdings.

Jason Ursaner: Sorry, I was on mute. Just on the Trio on the additional tons for next year and then kind of this road map for maybe additional 100,000 tons with moderate investment from there. Has that changed at all the marketability between the granular standard and fine langbeinite? Like are you adding any way to get additional tons of one? Or is it just kind of across the board?

Zachry Adams: Jason, thanks for the question. This is Zach. As we think about the additional tons of Trio, we see that growth coming from a variety of areas. First is focus on specialty crops like we talked about earlier and also where we see crops and soil types that have a broader recognition of sulfur and magnesium needs. And then with that growth, we see that as a combination of both market expansion and share gains. And within that, that expansion, that's geographically as well as customer base and also crop based, and we're currently working through and putting together plans for what that will look like into next year and beyond.

Kevin Crutchfield: And to the extent that the SOP project proceeds, that will be a source as well, as opposed to trying to find new markets in the U.S. or trying to grab market share or whatever. So that will be an outlet as well. To the extent the project proceeds.

Jason Ursaner: So for the SOP project, is it -- would you be using some of the standard and fine langbeinite as a raw input and then you don't have to market kind of the less desirable lower margin langbeinite because you could use that to create SOP, you could sell the higher margin granular and then kind of -- you have sort of an exchange reaction instead of a Mannheim process so you could get SOP and then also have mag chloride?

Kevin Crutchfield: Yes. No Mannheim process required here because we already have the sulfur on site. So the answer to your question is generally yes. That's how we're thinking about it, and that's how it work.

Jason Ursaner: Okay. Does it kind of increase your desire or willingness to try to expand the Trio production and have more of the standard and fine product, if you have an outlet for it, I guess, is what I'm eventually trying to get to?

Zachry Adams: Jason yes, absolutely. Absolutely. SOP drives the ability for us to grow our Trio production significantly more than it is today with providing a nice premium outlet for those fines into an upgraded specialty fertilizer product.

Jason Ursaner: Okay. And then, I guess, just a broader question for Kevin. You -- around $400 million market cap, $160 million of cash, you still have the $50 million eventually coming from Exxon. So it's around $190 million, $200 million of enterprise value just based on trailing numbers of EBITDA. I mean you're kind of trading 3.5x EBITDA or so. So the implication at least to me is either EBITDA is unsustainable, you're at some cyclical peak, you're structurally not converting EBITDA cash and none of those sound at all kind of what you're saying, which is pretty upbeat, optimistic and anything. So I guess from your perspective, what are -- I guess, what are people sort of missing here?

And what is going to change that in people's mind eventually for this being not only a sustainable business, but kind of an improving 1 pretty significantly is what it sounds like.

Kevin Crutchfield: Yes, that's an excellent question. I mean the way I think about it is start with the core assets. And we've been pounding the table for -- ever since I've been here about laser focus on core assets, getting them running better on an improved basis, more consistent, more reliable. And I think by any metric you look at over the last 2 to 4 years, that's a -- or a green check mark in that box. And then over time, too, the other thing that's happened is as we've continued to survey the asset base, you've got some new eyes looking at things here and there.

We're coming up with a lot of internal organic growth opportunities that we think are very investable that will have very nice returns on them. So I think you're right. I think maybe we're not telling the story, right? But this is a story of a very nice turnaround over a 2-, 3-year period with a lot of upside potential in the future. Now baseline with all that is we have to execute. We have to continue to do that quarter after quarter after quarter to regain sort of that credibility and that track record. But we think that there's tremendous upside here.

And I'm not going to speak to the share buying program exactly, but we upped our purchases when we saw weakness in the stock. And I think you could expect that to continue if you continue to see weakness in the stock because we think there's upside value here and it's a good value. So if a little frustration is coming through in my voice, should be, because I am a little bit but I also take the responsibility that we've got to tell the story better and make the value proposition more clear going forward because there's tremendous upside here.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Vitaly Kononov with Freedom Capital Markets.

Vitaly Kononov: So I'd like to maybe dissect on the cost divergence in the 2 segments. So we saw a year-over-year increase in Potash and year-over-year decrease in Trio. So maybe you can distinguish the factors that are driving the increase in Potash and explain some of the efficiency gains that helped to bring the cost of Trio down?

Kevin Crutchfield: Yes. Look, on the Trio side, as I mentioned earlier, that's an underground mine. We have continuous miner sections operating underground. The continuous miner loads coal into a shuttle cars, shuttle cars takes it to the belt. The belt takes it outside. We process it through the plant, and generate a salable product. All of that is a system. And what we've been doing is, as I said earlier, debottlenecking that system. Part of the problem early on was we had some continuous mining units that were older and experiencing low reliability, low availability, et cetera. So we replaced those, and that enhanced the system. But what it does is it points out, you've got a bottleneck somewhere else.

So we're just moving constraint to constraint across the site, and what that's led to is more operating time, higher productivity, more bits on langbeinite time in the face. The mill is operating really well. Our yields are higher, we're staying in the ore zone better. So all that has contributed to better production and better fixed cost absorption over the last couple of years. And I think the exciting thing about it is this is not the eighth inning of a ninth inning ball game, we're probably in the fourth inning here, on this thing. So I think it's got more runway, and we're excited to pursue it.

We're being very thoughtful about it because markets are somewhat fixed in the U.S., and we've got to think about proper outlets, and not destroying economic value as it relates to the value of the product in the marketplace. But we expect us to be very thoughtful around that approach over the next 2, 3 years but we're super excited about what that potential runway looks like.

Jason Tremblay: If I could add, Vitaly, just on your question on the Potash side. So -- the interesting part and the difference is, in Trio, we're ramping up one facility. So the cost performance is really visible based on kind of ramping that production and seeing the unit cost improvements for that facility. In Potash, right, we've got 3 facilities, and the production increases this year, the production improvement this year because we are improving production year-over-year in this year, but the improvements this year have largely been at 2 of our mines, HB and Wendover which are a higher cost facility than Moab, which is the third facility.

And so our production growth is happening at the 2 higher cost facilities. But at the same time, though, the cost per ton at those facilities is improving. And so the whole idea here for us is improved production at all of our facilities and drive better results. It doesn't show up in that consolidated cost per ton or COGS per ton measure because of that product mix. And that's what we've been trying to communicate. We are going to work and focus on better telling that story, moving into the future.

But I think what we see is improved cost performance at all the sites as the production ramps up, it's just the mix is making it difficult to see it on a consolidated level.

Vitaly Kononov: On the Wendover Lithium project, do I sense a change of sentiment here that the project could be the time lines of installing could be delayed somewhat, or am I guessing wrong?

Kevin Crutchfield: I mean relative to kind of where we started talking about this maybe a little bit, but they're still looking at definitive feasibility study by first quarter engineering continues, value-add engineering continues, FEL3 process is done, advanced discussions continue with offtake partners. That's actually going exceedingly well. So yes, but relative to maybe where we started a quarter or something, but it's not terrible, not to be unexpected in this space either.

Vitaly Kononov: All right. Got it. And the last question for me on the recent USDA announcements. I'm just curious what conditions are still remaining before the funding becomes binding? And how much customer offtake commitment would you require before approving construction?

Kevin Crutchfield: So we're just in the early stages of finalizing that work with the USDA. I suspect that will take a good bit of time. And as it relates to what we'd want to have presold before we gave the green light. I think that's part and parcel to the final investment decision process, what the markets look like, where we can move the tons, as you know, a lot of this product is an import product, which we think we could displace but that would be part of the final investment decision, along with final CapEx, what's the cost structure look like et cetera, et cetera.

So in the next -- over the course of the next 8 to 12 months, we have a lot of work to do, and we'll be able to update you in the coming quarters on how that work is shaping up.

Operator: This concludes the question-and-answer session. I would like to turn the conference back over to Kevin Crutchfield for any closing remarks.

Kevin Crutchfield: Thank you, operator. Once again, thanks to everybody for your interest for tuning in to today's call. If you have any questions in the future, please reach out. If you're shy, you can just hit the investor website at [email protected], and we'll certainly follow up with you. Thank you, and talk to you next quarter.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. You may disconnect your lines. Thank you for participating, and have a pleasant day.

#3257. Pliant raises $80M to open its B2B payments platform to AI agents

Claude, ChatGPT and in-house AI agents can now run business payments through Pliant. The Berlin fintech, past $100M in recurring revenue, will expand in North America.

Pliant co-founders Malte Rau and Fabian Terner

The money will fund Pliant’s expansion in the US and Canada, its entry into further markets and its AI roadmap. The round follows three years in which Pliant doubled its business each year. It comes shortly after the company passed $100M in annual recurring revenue.

Pliant combines commercial card issuing, payment accounts, foreign exchange and spend management in one platform. Its own AI agents already automate recurring finance work for customers.

Outside agents, from Claude and ChatGPT to a company’s own automations, connect through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). They can then run payment workflows inside other business processes, with permissions, controls and audit trails built in, Pliant says.

“Whether an established business wants AI to automate its payment processes with the right guardrails, or an AI-native company needs a licensed partner that moves as fast as it does, Pliant is built for that,” said Malte Rau, Pliant’s CEO and co-founder.

Pliant started in 2020 and is a principal member of Visa and Mastercard. It issues commercial cards in 13 currencies across 32 countries under its European e-money licence, and through regulated partners in the UK and US. It employs more than 300 people across eight offices.

Its customers include travel, insurance and AI-native companies. Banks, fintechs and software platforms also use its infrastructure to run their own commercial card offerings.

“When agents move money, someone still has to be licensed, auditable and liable, and that is the layer Pliant owns,” said Vinoth Jayakumar, general partner at Seaya Nova, in the Business Wire release.

Card networks are testing agent payments too. In October, AI agents started paying supplier invoices in a pilot with Visa, BILL and Billtrust. Synchrony wants to put store cards inside ChatGPT. In corporate cards, US rival Ramp reached a $60bn valuation in October.

#3256. Apple announces Fitness+ Gym Strength program with personalized workout plans

Apple wants to help you get stronger. Apple Fitness+ is expanding to the gym with a new strength training experience. Gym Strength is now available in beta, bringing personalized workout plans, exercise demonstrations, and Apple Watch logging to your lifting routine.

Gym Strength creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment. After you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weight you logged.

The feature is designed for a range of experience levels, from people trying strength training for the first time to experienced lifters looking to make progress. It also aims to help anyone who wants to build a more consistent routine.

When building a plan, you choose your workout days and the body areas you want to focus on. You can select five exercises per workout, which Apple estimates will take about 20–30 minutes, or seven exercises for about 45–60 minutes, depending on your pace.

Each workout recommends exercises, reps, sets, and how much weight to lift.

You move through the workout at your own pace, with short video demonstrations from Apple Fitness+ trainers available for each exercise. The demonstrations can be expanded to show the movement from three different angles.

Apple says Gym Strength includes over 350 exercises across more than 30 types of strength training equipment, including dumbbells, kettlebells, suspension trainers, cable machines, and barbells. Dumbbells are the minimum equipment requirement.

Plans account for the equipment available to you, so the experience can work in a commercial gym or a home gym.

If a machine is occupied or you’re training somewhere with different equipment, you can swap equipment or choose an alternative exercise with a similar movement and body focus. You can also add sets or skip exercises.

Gym Strength requires an iPhone running iOS 27.3 or an iPad running iPadOS 27.3. An Apple Watch running watchOS 27.3 optionally lets you view exercises and log reps and weight from your wrist, while tracking heart rate and calories burned.

Gym Strength also introduces Training Note, an optional feature powered by Apple Intelligence that previews workouts, explains progression, and highlights milestones. Training Note requires an Apple Intelligence–enabled iPhone or iPad with the device set to English.

Gym Strength is included in the existing Fitness+ subscription. It joins a library of trainer-led workouts spanning 12 workout types, including Strength, HIIT, Yoga, Pilates, Core, Cycling, Rowing, Dance, Kickboxing, treadmill walking and running, and Mindful Cooldown.

Fitness+ also offers guided meditations, personalized recommendations, and Custom Plans for scheduling workouts, with new sessions added every week.

Fitness+ is also included in Apple One Premier, which costs $39.95 per month in the U.S. and bundles Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Arcade, Apple News+, and 2TB of iCloud+ storage.

#3255. Why Engineers Should Brave Capitol Hill

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Congress needs accurate technical insights

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum.

During this year’s Congressional Visits Day, Nikhil Jathar [second from left] and three other IEEE members met with Nile Whitmore [middle], a legislative assistant for Representative Greg Casar (D-Texas).

When San Antonio–based software engineer Nikhil Jathar first went to Washington, D.C., to advocate for federal support for technology education and research funding, he was in awe of the opportunity. It was spring of 2025, not long after Jathar settled in the United States from India, when he got an invitation to join the annual Congressional Visits Day organized by IEEE-USA.

“My first reaction was, ‘Wow, I get to visit Congress,’ ” says Jathar, CTO of AvanSaber, a business software company he cofounded in 2014. At the time, he did not have a specific lobbying position on behalf of the company. But he was intrigued by the invitation—which goes out to all U.S. IEEE members—and as he read more about congressional visits, his motivation deepened. He realized: “I need to try this. I want to see where it goes.”

What’s Your Ask? Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:Cosponsor (or oppose) an existing bill or amendment.Preserve, remove, or modify legislative text in a bill under consideration.Add language to an appropriations bill or committee report.Ask a federal agency a specific oversight question.Request a briefing, hearing, Government Accountability Office review, or stakeholder roundtable.Encourage an agency to clarify a technical rule.

Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:

Congressional staffers say they welcome the knowledge and perspective that engineers like Jathar and other visitors from beyond Washington, D.C., provide. It’s also important for those visitors to be clear on what they are advocating for. One staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, who agreed to speak anonymously due to the office’s media policy, says, “Ideas for new policies come from multiple places. It could begin at the [legislator] or staff level, an ask from a constituent, or needs from industry. It’s up to us to figure out what would do the most good,” the staffer said. “For instance, if you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”

For engineers in the United States, speaking with elected representatives is an effective way to shape key policies, but it takes some preparation and the right approach, as Jathar learned over the course of two visits.

Congress’s job is to act on behalf of the people, and it has rules for how people can lobby it. It distinguishes between broader advocacy—conversations between constituents and U.S. representatives—and professional lobbying, which involves paid professionals and is governed by the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Many professional groups like IEEE also organize congressional visits for their members. Those visits can be subject to lobbying rules, so the organizers told Jathar that: “You are representing the organization, not your own views.” He would need to stick to the talking points IEEE-USA had prepared for all its participants, regardless of their specialty, to promote across several congressional offices.

On Jathar’s first visit, those organizational talking points included advocating for funding smart grids, authorizing Department of Energy research, and investing in STEM education. That represents one of the trade-offs of access in Washington. IEEE-USA’s priorities didn’t all overlap directly with Jathar’s work, but they were broad enablers of science and technology and, he says, “STEM education funding is close to my heart.”

Anyone can approach their representatives in Washington with their personal priorities, Jathar notes, but given how pressed for time congressional staff are, they are more likely to prioritize a meeting that represents the views of as many of their constituents as possible. “I could have gone outside the IEEE structure,” Jathar says, but congressional staff “are more likely to listen if you are part of a much bigger organization.”

For Jathar’s first congressional visit, organizers assigned him to call on the offices of several representatives from both political parties based on where he lives: Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), and Barry Moore (R-Ala.). “Meeting a staffer or a senior member from their office is good. They tend to relate to these issues more than a representative, because a representative has 10 different high-level things they have to worry about whereas the staffer can be more focused on the policy details,” Jathar says.

A typical visit like this may last anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour, so Jathar kept his talking points simple and short. “First and foremost you’re gonna get a very small window,” he says, “Make sure you’ve got everything ready to present in bullet points and not a lot of jargon. You can always bring that out later if they ask more questions.” Simple visual aids, in the form of one-page handouts, may be helpful for communicating numeric or technical information, too.

“If you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”–Staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology

The House Science Committee staffer agrees: “I prefer meetings where people know what they want and know what we’re doing in Congress.” In addition to having a clear request, the staffer says engineers and other advocates should keep track of where Congress is in its cycle: Is it appropriations season, and when is the next budget being set? How far along is a given piece of legislation in the process, and what is realistic to change at that point?

During Jathar’s 2025 visit to one Capitol Hill office, he learned firsthand the importance of preparation. For one of the three representatives he visited, staff politely pointed out that the legislator they worked for was not on the committee with jurisdiction over the IEEE-USA talking point they were discussing. “They explained that there are only certain things [the legislator] can do on that issue and that there are other people we need to talk to, to achieve more,” Jathar recalls.

Earlier this year, Jathar decided to go back to Capitol Hill with his newfound knowledge, again within the framework of an IEEE-USA visit. This time he was able to provide something else legislative staff want from engineers: authoritative technical knowledge.

“When I introduced myself as a software developer to one staffer, his first question was, ‘Do you think AI will replace coders?’ ” Jathar says. The conversation went back and forth, with the staffer asking Jathar and his other engineering companions questions. Jathar went on to explain that his company developed an open-source business-management software it calls ERPClaw, designed to be used with AI agents such as OpenClaw. That led naturally to discussing the role of open source in AI, which plays a role in one of IEEE-USA’s proposals for democratizing AI. This time Jathar was able to align his organization’s advocacy with his expertise and the staffer’s areas of interest.

It’s too soon to know what legislative impact that advocacy might have, but it’s the sort of informed, relevant proposal that legislative staff seek out. “The people who build trust have more cachet with congressional staff because they’ve asked for something that’s reasonably thought out,” the House Science Committee staffer says. In turn, congressional staffers can advocate better within their offices for policies brought to them by people they trust.

And talking about the issues you care the most about can deepen that trust. The House Science Committee staffer once visited Congress as an advocate before switching to the other side of the table. On that visit, as on Jathar’s, the professional society organizing the visit provided a pitch. “I was making a pitch that was given to me without a lot of personal buy-in,” the staffer says. Instead, “you should feel emotionally connected to any issue you’re advocating for.”

Jathar’s support for the open-source movement is like that. Open source gives smaller companies a foundation they can adapt and build upon, while allowing other developers to extend that work. “We can progress a lot faster,” Jathar says. “I’m not doing it only because it’s good for my business, but because I feel it’s good for any technological advancement.”

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum. He covers how emerging technologies are changing the balance of power between companies, governments, and individuals. The rest of the time, he worries about his own balance on a bicycle, skis, or the side of a mountain.

I found it difficult to get answers from legislative offices, so I'd love to hear what's missing in this story from any legislative staffers either here in the comments or at my email address (on our About page). I also know that things work somewhat differently in each country--are there readers in India or Germany or Chile who might be able to share their experiences working with lawmakers there?
