#3227. How Beta Technologies Is Clearing the Runway for Electric Flight

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

It aims to lift the industry with its aircraft, motors, batteries, and charging network

Beta Technologies, one of the top three U.S. electric aircraft makers, is aiming first at regional cargo and medical transport, before pursuing the passenger market. Shown here is Beta’s Alia A250, for vertical takeoffs and landings.

In the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont. Cleared for takeoff, he releases the brakes and nudges the throttle forward.

At the back of the aircraft, the five-blade pusher propeller snaps awake, and the Alia bolts forward. There’s no shriek of a turbofan spooling up, no shudder of a piston engine, and no wait for thrust. Just the low hum of an electric motor and a shove of instant acceleration.

Within a few seconds, we’re at 85 knots (almost 160 kilometers per hour), and Caputo rotates the nose upward. The runway drops abruptly away as we climb. Gaining speed and altitude, we head northwest over Lake Champlain. Through the wraparound canopy, I watch the hunched shoulders of Vermont’s Green Mountains shrink under the right wing, with New York’s taller Adirondacks to the left.

Caputo, a former Air Force fighter pilot, flicks the control stick hard left, then right. Despite its 15-meter wingspan, the Alia feels snappy, its fly-by-wire system automatically coordinating aileron and rudder inputs. The machine, he says, is much simpler to manage than the Cessna 182 I flew around Australia in my student-pilot days.

What’s more, our half-hour flight in the Alia will consume only about US $9 worth of electricity. The same flight in a comparable Cessna 208 Caravan would burn roughly 25 to 30 gallons of Jet A fuel, costing about $210 to $255 at press time. “Even at full throttle, we’re not burning any fuel up here,” says Caputo, as he takes the Alia into a sweeping left turn and heads south over the lake. “We’re not polluting the environment. [There’s] no noise pollution.”

At Beta’s South Burlington, Vt., facility, workers assemble the body of an Alia A250. The company says it has an order and option-to-buy backlog of nearly 1,000 aircraft.Beta Technologies

This ride is happening during an unusually lively time for electric aviation. The promise of lower operating costs and cleaner flight has pushed electric aircraft from a fringe experiment to one of the aviation industry’s most closely watched frontiers. After years of renderings, prototypes, and overly optimistic timetables, companies are now flying full-size aircraft, submitting hardware to regulators for certification, building factories, and testing routes with prospective customers.

Among the top three U.S. developers of electric planes, Archer Aviation and Joby Aviation are concentrating on piloted vertical-takeoff-and-landing air taxis, otherwise known as eVTOLs. Beta Technologies is taking a broader—and in some ways more innovative—path into the market. Rather than betting first on air taxis, Beta is looking to enter electric aviation through short-haul freight planes that use conventional runways, fed by an open charging network that’s designed to make electric aircraft—both Beta’s and its competitors’—part of a working transportation system.

To that end, the company is developing two variants of its Alia airframe: the runway-based CX300 I’m flying in and the A250, which adds four lift propellers for vertical takeoff and landing. Beta says its test pilots have flown the Alia family more than 300,000 kilometers, including doing multiple U.S. crossings and overseas demonstrations. The company claims an order and option-to-buy backlog of 991 aircraft.

RELATED: From Hockey Enforcer to High-Flying eVTOL CEO

“We’re taking a pragmatic stepwise approach for both certification and market entry,” says Beta’s CEO and founder Kyle Clark. “We’re ready to go today with medical and cargo aircraft that fly from airport to airport.” Next up, he says, will be passenger aircraft with conventional takeoff and landing, followed by cargo eVTOLs, and finally passenger eVTOLs.

Beta’s 17,500-square-meter production facility sits beside the Burlington airport and looks more like a giant sunlit workshop than a conventional airplane factory. Geothermal heat pumps help heat and cool the structure. The roof will eventually hold a megawatt of solar panels. On the floor, technicians make composite structures and join aircraft sections beneath American and Pride flags.

3 Competing Paths to Electric AviationThe top three U.S. electric-aircraft makers are taking different approaches to the same challenge: how to make short-hop flight cleaner, quieter, and commercially useful.aspect_ratioJoby Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger S4 aircraft has six tilting propellers to provide both vertical lift and cruise propulsion. It’s optimized for fast, quiet air-taxi service. The company is also working on hydrogen fuel cells for longer-range transport. Joby says the S4 is in the final stage of the Federal Aviation Administration’s certification process and has flown trials in Dubai, New York, and Texas.Archer Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger Midnight has 12 propellers—six tilting rotors and six stationary rotors. The aircraft, which Archer has been testing in both vertical and conventional takeoffs and landings, is aimed at air-taxi service in urban areas. The company says Midnight is in Phase 4 of the FAA certification process and has completed trial flights.Beta Technologies’ piloted Alia aircraft comes in two flavors: The A250 eVTOL has separate vertical-lift rotors and a rear cruise propeller, while the CX300 is a conventional-takeoff fixed-wing plane. The two models use the same pusher motor, battery pack, flight control computer, and fixed-pitch propeller. The company is initially focusing on cargo and medical transport, regional logistics, and airport-to-airport operations, with passenger service later. Beta expects FAA certification for the CX300 in 2027 and for the A250 a year later.Kyle Clark, a native of Vermont, founded Beta in 2017 to realize his long-held dream of building a hybrid-electric aircraft. (For his bachelor’s thesis at Harvard University, he designed a flight-control system for such an aircraft.) Martine Rothblatt, CEO of the biotech company United Therapeutics and cofounder of SiriusXM satellite radio, invested $48 million in Beta to fund its first prototype, with the eventual goal of using the aircraft to transport organs for transplantation.The company has kept much of its design and manufacturing in-house, partly because the pieces are closely coupled and partly because suitable aviation components didn’t exist when development began. Vertical integration gives Beta’s engineers control over the interfaces and any failure data. But it also means the company must be competent at several businesses simultaneously: airframes, electric motors, inverters, batteries, software, chargers, and aircraft production.The production line can build both the fixed-wing CX300 and the vertical-lift A250, which share the same fuselage, wings, pusher motor (for horizontal propulsion), batteries, avionics, and much of the tooling. This results in some one-size-fits-all decisions: The CX300’s twin booms, which connect the wing to the tail surfaces, look superfluous until you see the A250’s four lift propellers mounted on similar structures.On the CX300, those booms add weight and drag even though they serve no lift function. But the trade-off—a simpler overall design—is part of Beta’s central strategy: Rather than applying for FAA certification for the more novel and complex eVTOL A250, with its multiple lift systems and transitions between hover and wing-borne flight, the company is bringing the runway version forward first. It’s certifying the motor, batteries, fly-by-wire controls, and much of the airframe in the simpler aircraft; it will then reuse evidence and manufacturing experience when it certifies the A250.The other big reason to start with the CX300 is logistical: The United States has more than 5,000 public-use airports, so the CX300 can operate from infrastructure that already exists. The cargo and medical flights that the aircraft will initially tackle offer tightly defined missions in which lower energy and maintenance costs matter more than cabin amenities. Hence the company’s decision to leave cabin air-conditioning off the CX300, at least for now. “Things that don’t exist on an airplane don’t weigh anything,” Clark says. “They can’t break. You don’t have to service them…. You don’t have to certify them.”“This strategy, at the beginning, was seen as a failure of their VTOL,” says analyst Sergio Cecutta, a managing partner at SMG Consulting. “But I think a lot of people were very myopic. It was a way for [Beta] to break up the certification in two pieces, and so they have retired a lot of the risk. [A majority] of the [CX300’s] parts are shared with the VTOL, and that means that a lot of the documentation for certification can be easily reused on the VTOL side when that certification starts.”How Redundancy Enhances SafetyA decade and a half after electric cars began making significant inroads into the automotive market, electric airplane technology is advancing rapidly. In some ways, an electric car has more complicated power-engineering requirements than an electric aircraft. An electric car’s power demands change constantly, while an electric aircraft operates in a narrower set of power regimes: takeoff, level flight, and descent.But if your car’s drivetrain fails, you can just pull over to the side of the road. That’s not an option for a pilot 1,000 meters up. The hurdle isn’t that electric motors are inherently fragile; it’s that aviation safety standards are extraordinarily demanding. Catastrophic failure conditions generally must be held to roughly one chance in a billion flight hours or less.The two versions of Beta’s Alia aircraft—the A250 [shown] and the CX300—share many of the same components, which the company believes will speed up FAA certification.Beta TechnologiesBecause individual electrical components cannot meet that standard on their own, electric aircraft rely on layered redundancy: duplicate power paths, independent inverters, fault isolation, monitoring, and backup capacity. Each layer helps close the safety gap, but each also adds weight and complexity.To close the reliability gap and satisfy regulators who have little experience with electric aircraft, Beta engineers have built redundancy into the motor itself. When I visit the company’s motor shop, technicians are assembling the H500A pusher motor, which splits up critical components like the inverters and stator sections.“You could lose an entire half of the system, and it would still function the same,” says Adam Lowe, Beta’s flight operations lead.The H500A’s broad diameter gives the magnetic forces greater leverage, producing high torque at low rotational speed, a useful trait when turning large propellers. The H500A weighs about 75 kilograms and produces about 640 kilowatts of power. The motor achieves 97.5 percent efficiency, based on internal testing; typical conventional turboprops have an efficiency range of 25 to 35 percent.Beta had aimed to have its motor certified in the first half of 2026, a deadline that passed without a public announcement. Although the company’s certification strategy is aimed at streamlining the process, getting clearance to fly from the Federal Aviation Administration is probably still its biggest obstacle. For Beta, and any company trying to bring an electric aircraft into service, the FAA must sign off first on the propeller, then the motor, then the aircraft. After that, the manufacturer must pursue a production certificate from the FAA, proving that the company can build the same approved aircraft again and again, with the right tools, records, inspections, quality controls, supplier oversight, training, calibration, and parts tracking.Beta has found a narrow on-ramp to get the A250 flying before full certification. Under the FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, companies and public agencies can run FAA-supervised, real-world trials to test how advanced air-mobility aircraft might operate in the national airspace. For Beta, that included July flights of the CX300 across a Virginia-to-Maryland corridor carrying, among other things, a manufactured transplantable organ in a medical containment system. Beta has also been chosen for six other FAA-backed trials.For the fixed-wing Alia CX300, customer trials are moving in parallel. In March, Beta’s CX300 successfully completed 23 flights over 10 days on Loganair routes linking six Scottish cities. The airline has since signed a term sheet for five Beta aircraft, with options for five more and service expected to start in 2029.Innovation in eVTOLsBeta is pushing so hard for the A250 because the case for electric flight gets even more interesting with vertical-lift aircraft. Helicopters and other VTOLs have a less orderly life than fixed-wing planes do. They must hover, sidestep, turn in place, settle, climb, and hold themselves in the air by main force. But conventional helicopters are built around a rotor speed that varies only a few percent because the engine, transmission, and rotor system are all designed around one narrow operating point.“One of the dreams of vertical flight has been to vary the rotor rpm,” says Anubhav Datta, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, who studies electric propulsion and vertical flight. Electric motors, he argues, have advanced enough to make that practical. A rotor that can slow down or speed up as conditions change can waste less energy, make less noise, and better match the odd assortment of tasks that vertical flight demands.Electric propulsion also lets designers break up the work with multiple motors. The weight of an electric motor is tied closely to its torque. If you spread that torque among several motors, each of the motors can shrink, meaning that their combined weight is less than would be needed for one big engine. This is one reason why so many electric aircraft designs appear to have sprouted propellers wherever an engineer found a place to put one.There is a downside to using multiple smaller motors: If one of the motors quits, the rotor it’s driving has little stored energy compared to the inertia in a conventional helicopter’s one large rotor. This inertia can come in handy if the engine dies, because the rotor will continue to spin and allow the pilot to descend under control, in an emergency technique known as autorotation. Beta Technologies, Made in Vermont Beta TechnologiesAccording to Beta Technologies founder and CEO Kyle Clark, his native Vermont—known more for its maple syrup and outdoorsy lifestyle than its technological achievements—is a big part of the secret to Beta’s success at attracting talent. “The recruiting strategy is this: You find anybody who has vacationed in Vermont or went to school here. And you say, ‘You can actually live here and have a high-paying job in a mission-driven business, doing something that you care about with great people.’ ” The company currently employs about 1,500 people, most of them in South Burlington, Vt., and is actively hiring for its engineering, manufacturing, software, flight operations, and commercial teams.As befits an aviation company, Beta offers flying lessons for all employees—a perk that is intended to give engineers, software developers, pilots, and mechanics a common language. The company also operates a health clinic for employees and their families and is building a day care center. Those programs have an idealistic Vermont flavor that is shaped by Clark and his wife, Katie Clark, who is Beta’s head of brand, creative, culture and spaces. But they also serve a practical purpose: attracting and retaining the best people in a small labor market. —T.C.

The top three U.S. electric-aircraft makers are taking different approaches to the same challenge: how to make short-hop flight cleaner, quieter, and commercially useful.

Kyle Clark, a native of Vermont, founded Beta in 2017 to realize his long-held dream of building a hybrid-electric aircraft. (For his bachelor’s thesis at Harvard University, he designed a flight-control system for such an aircraft.) Martine Rothblatt, CEO of the biotech company United Therapeutics and cofounder of SiriusXM satellite radio, invested $48 million in Beta to fund its first prototype, with the eventual goal of using the aircraft to transport organs for transplantation.

The company has kept much of its design and manufacturing in-house, partly because the pieces are closely coupled and partly because suitable aviation components didn’t exist when development began. Vertical integration gives Beta’s engineers control over the interfaces and any failure data. But it also means the company must be competent at several businesses simultaneously: airframes, electric motors, inverters, batteries, software, chargers, and aircraft production.

The production line can build both the fixed-wing CX300 and the vertical-lift A250, which share the same fuselage, wings, pusher motor (for horizontal propulsion), batteries, avionics, and much of the tooling. This results in some one-size-fits-all decisions: The CX300’s twin booms, which connect the wing to the tail surfaces, look superfluous until you see the A250’s four lift propellers mounted on similar structures.

On the CX300, those booms add weight and drag even though they serve no lift function. But the trade-off—a simpler overall design—is part of Beta’s central strategy: Rather than applying for FAA certification for the more novel and complex eVTOL A250, with its multiple lift systems and transitions between hover and wing-borne flight, the company is bringing the runway version forward first. It’s certifying the motor, batteries, fly-by-wire controls, and much of the airframe in the simpler aircraft; it will then reuse evidence and manufacturing experience when it certifies the A250.

The other big reason to start with the CX300 is logistical: The United States has more than 5,000 public-use airports, so the CX300 can operate from infrastructure that already exists. The cargo and medical flights that the aircraft will initially tackle offer tightly defined missions in which lower energy and maintenance costs matter more than cabin amenities. Hence the company’s decision to leave cabin air-conditioning off the CX300, at least for now. “Things that don’t exist on an airplane don’t weigh anything,” Clark says. “They can’t break. You don’t have to service them…. You don’t have to certify them.”

“This strategy, at the beginning, was seen as a failure of their VTOL,” says analyst Sergio Cecutta, a managing partner at SMG Consulting. “But I think a lot of people were very myopic. It was a way for [Beta] to break up the certification in two pieces, and so they have retired a lot of the risk. [A majority] of the [CX300’s] parts are shared with the VTOL, and that means that a lot of the documentation for certification can be easily reused on the VTOL side when that certification starts.”

A decade and a half after electric cars began making significant inroads into the automotive market, electric airplane technology is advancing rapidly. In some ways, an electric car has more complicated power-engineering requirements than an electric aircraft. An electric car’s power demands change constantly, while an electric aircraft operates in a narrower set of power regimes: takeoff, level flight, and descent.

But if your car’s drivetrain fails, you can just pull over to the side of the road. That’s not an option for a pilot 1,000 meters up. The hurdle isn’t that electric motors are inherently fragile; it’s that aviation safety standards are extraordinarily demanding. Catastrophic failure conditions generally must be held to roughly one chance in a billion flight hours or less.

The two versions of Beta’s Alia aircraft—the A250 [shown] and the CX300—share many of the same components, which the company believes will speed up FAA certification.

Because individual electrical components cannot meet that standard on their own, electric aircraft rely on layered redundancy: duplicate power paths, independent inverters, fault isolation, monitoring, and backup capacity. Each layer helps close the safety gap, but each also adds weight and complexity.

To close the reliability gap and satisfy regulators who have little experience with electric aircraft, Beta engineers have built redundancy into the motor itself. When I visit the company’s motor shop, technicians are assembling the H500A pusher motor, which splits up critical components like the inverters and stator sections.

“You could lose an entire half of the system, and it would still function the same,” says Adam Lowe, Beta’s flight operations lead.

The H500A’s broad diameter gives the magnetic forces greater leverage, producing high torque at low rotational speed, a useful trait when turning large propellers. The H500A weighs about 75 kilograms and produces about 640 kilowatts of power. The motor achieves 97.5 percent efficiency, based on internal testing; typical conventional turboprops have an efficiency range of 25 to 35 percent.

Beta had aimed to have its motor certified in the first half of 2026, a deadline that passed without a public announcement. Although the company’s certification strategy is aimed at streamlining the process, getting clearance to fly from the Federal Aviation Administration is probably still its biggest obstacle. For Beta, and any company trying to bring an electric aircraft into service, the FAA must sign off first on the propeller, then the motor, then the aircraft. After that, the manufacturer must pursue a production certificate from the FAA, proving that the company can build the same approved aircraft again and again, with the right tools, records, inspections, quality controls, supplier oversight, training, calibration, and parts tracking.

Beta has found a narrow on-ramp to get the A250 flying before full certification. Under the FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, companies and public agencies can run FAA-supervised, real-world trials to test how advanced air-mobility aircraft might operate in the national airspace. For Beta, that included July flights of the CX300 across a Virginia-to-Maryland corridor carrying, among other things, a manufactured transplantable organ in a medical containment system. Beta has also been chosen for six other FAA-backed trials.

For the fixed-wing Alia CX300, customer trials are moving in parallel. In March, Beta’s CX300 successfully completed 23 flights over 10 days on Loganair routes linking six Scottish cities. The airline has since signed a term sheet for five Beta aircraft, with options for five more and service expected to start in 2029.

Beta is pushing so hard for the A250 because the case for electric flight gets even more interesting with vertical-lift aircraft. Helicopters and other VTOLs have a less orderly life than fixed-wing planes do. They must hover, sidestep, turn in place, settle, climb, and hold themselves in the air by main force. But conventional helicopters are built around a rotor speed that varies only a few percent because the engine, transmission, and rotor system are all designed around one narrow operating point.

“One of the dreams of vertical flight has been to vary the rotor rpm,” says Anubhav Datta, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, who studies electric propulsion and vertical flight. Electric motors, he argues, have advanced enough to make that practical. A rotor that can slow down or speed up as conditions change can waste less energy, make less noise, and better match the odd assortment of tasks that vertical flight demands.

Electric propulsion also lets designers break up the work with multiple motors. The weight of an electric motor is tied closely to its torque. If you spread that torque among several motors, each of the motors can shrink, meaning that their combined weight is less than would be needed for one big engine. This is one reason why so many electric aircraft designs appear to have sprouted propellers wherever an engineer found a place to put one.

There is a downside to using multiple smaller motors: If one of the motors quits, the rotor it’s driving has little stored energy compared to the inertia in a conventional helicopter’s one large rotor. This inertia can come in handy if the engine dies, because the rotor will continue to spin and allow the pilot to descend under control, in an emergency technique known as autorotation.

According to Beta Technologies founder and CEO Kyle Clark, his native Vermont—known more for its maple syrup and outdoorsy lifestyle than its technological achievements—is a big part of the secret to Beta’s success at attracting talent. “The recruiting strategy is this: You find anybody who has vacationed in Vermont or went to school here. And you say, ‘You can actually live here and have a high-paying job in a mission-driven business, doing something that you care about with great people.’ ” The company currently employs about 1,500 people, most of them in South Burlington, Vt., and is actively hiring for its engineering, manufacturing, software, flight operations, and commercial teams.

As befits an aviation company, Beta offers flying lessons for all employees—a perk that is intended to give engineers, software developers, pilots, and mechanics a common language. The company also operates a health clinic for employees and their families and is building a day care center. Those programs have an idealistic Vermont flavor that is shaped by Clark and his wife, Katie Clark, who is Beta’s head of brand, creative, culture and spaces. But they also serve a practical purpose: attracting and retaining the best people in a small labor market. —T.C.

Electric-aircraft makers compensate with redundant motors and electrical channels, but most leading designs also have wings to allow gliding. In Beta’s A250, that means that if all else fails, the pilot still has a shot at reaching a suitable landing spot.

That helps explain the convergence in today’s eVTOL designs. Joby Aviation’s S4 uses six propellers that tilt between lift and cruise. Archer Aviation’s Midnight has six tilting propellers and six dedicated lift props. Beta’s A250 keeps its four lift propellers horizontal and uses a separate pusher motor for forward flight.

In Beta’s home state of Vermont, the electricity produced in the state comes almost entirely from renewable sources. Of course, electric aviation’s climate advantage depends not only on how clean the power grid is, but on how efficiently the aircraft uses energy. The turbines in conventional jet engines are marvelous machines, but they throw away a lot of energy as heat. Plus they need to carry the hardware to manage that heat—inlets, ducts, radiators, oil coolers—and the drag that comes with pulling air through all of it.

Kyle Clark [in cockpit], founder and CEO of Beta Technologies, pilots the company’s Alia CX300, an electric plane that Beta expects to receive FAA certification in 2027. Clark began designing a hybrid electric plane while still in college.Beta Technologies

By contrast, an electric design, with no combustion, gearbox, or oil circuits, avoids much of that energy burden. The result is an aircraft that is more than twice as “slippery” in terms of its lift-to-drag ratio. Batteries will never come close to the fuel density of petroleum fuels. But because electric drivetrains are much more efficient than combustion engines, a battery doesn’t necessarily need to match the energy density of petroleum fuel to be useful.

While the motors on an electric aircraft provide the drama at takeoff and landing, the batteries set nearly every boundary: the range, payload, charge time, cooling load, reserve energy, and, ultimately, useful life. For now, the hardest limit on electric aviation is not imagination, software, or even motors. It is the stubborn weight of stored energy.

“One thing you notice about [electric] airplanes is that they are all small,” says Cecutta, the aviation analyst. “They are not small because someone has done a market study and decided that is the optimal size. They are small because you cannot make them big. This limitation is from the batteries.”

In a conventional aircraft, fuel accounts for a significant percentage of the takeoff weight. But that weight gradually disappears during flight. In an electric plane, the battery packs also account for a lot of the weight; in Beta’s CX300, they’re close to half the aircraft’s mass. But a drained battery at landing weighs the same as a fully charged one at takeoff. That means the rest of the aircraft must be light enough to lift a power source that never gets lighter, yet strong enough to endure vibration, turbulence, hard landings, and years of fatigue. The more engineers push to save weight, Datta notes, the more flexible the airframe becomes, making the wings and other structures more prone to bending, twisting, and vibration. In that sense, the battery problem becomes a structural problem, too.

Beta’s CX300 carries five liquid-cooled battery packs of about 45 kilowatt-hours each, giving the aircraft roughly 225 kWh of rated capacity, though not all of that may be usable in flight. Each pack weighs 255 kg and contains 2,772 cylindrical cells. Altogether, about 14,000 cells sit beneath the occupied cabin, each one a tiny storehouse of energy, heat, and potential trouble.

The burden of the battery explains much of what I see elsewhere in Beta’s aircraft: the 15-meter wingspan, the composite structure, and the almost doctrinal effort to leave out every piece of hardware and creature comfort that’s not essential to the mission. The CX300 even does without flaps, which most aircraft use to generate extra lift at low speeds, so it must take off and land unusually fast for an aircraft of its size.

On Beta’s battery line, commercially supplied standard 21-millimeter-diameter, 70-mm-long cells are tested and assembled. Cells become modules, modules become subpacks, and eleven subpacks become a 45-kWh pack. Cooling plates manage heat during normal operation, while passive barriers and electrical isolation are designed to contain the ugly edge cases that Beta’s testing process intentionally triggers.

The modular design of the packs will give Beta’s planes a path to better batteries as the cells and battery chemistry improve. Caputo tells me that the company is already evaluating higher-density cells at its battery testing facility in nearby St. Albans, Vt. More watt-hours per kilogram could eventually mean more range, more payload, or both.

What sets Beta Technologies apart from its competitors is the breadth of its ambitions: It’s not just building electric aircraft. It’s also cultivating a broader ecosystem to nurture the growth of electric aviation.

For instance, Beta intends its motor business to extend beyond its own aircraft. The company has delivered lift motors for Eve Air Mobility’s proof-of-concept aircraft and has a contract to supply up to $1 billion in pusher motors as Eve’s program develops. In addition, Beta is selling flight-control computers and software to Horizon Aircraft. It is also producing propulsion systems for the military, as well as the MV250, a hybrid-electric autonomous aircraft for defense missions.

Beta’s fast-charging stations [left] have been installed at 138 locations. The thermal-management station [right] keeps the battery from overheating during charging. The company uses the open-standard Combined Charging System (CCS) so that other aircraft can use its chargers. Beta Technologies

Further evidence of Beta’s far-ranging plans is visible near the battery line in the South Burlington facility, where workers are readying a few of the company’s 1.5-meter-tall Charge Cubes for shipping. Intended for installation at airports, each cube takes 480-volt AC from the grid and can deliver up to 320 kW at as much as 1,000 volts DC. According to Beta, charging either model of its Alia aircraft takes about 35 minutes, from the minimum charge required under visual flight rules to full state. A separate thermal-management cube circulates water-glycol coolant through the aircraft to keep the batteries from overheating during charging.

The charge cubes use the Combined Charging System (CCS), an open standard increasingly shared across the electric transportation industry. Beta’s strategy resembles Tesla’s decision to treat charging as part of the vehicle business, with one important difference: Beta is courting other aircraft makers, airports, and operators to use its technology. Archer, Atlantic Aviation, Signature Aviation, and government agencies have purchased or installed Beta’s charging equipment. As of October, Beta has 138 fast-charge locations, with additional sites in permitting or construction.

For charging beyond the fixed network, Beta offers a wheeled 40-kW Mini Cube and a 65-kW Mini Cube+ that can ride inside an Alia and plug into more modest electrical service. The Mini Cube can also charge cars, buses, and trucks—any vehicle that uses the CCS standard.

Back above Lake Champlain, the CX300 levels off, and the motor recedes to a faint hum. Then Caputo switches it off, and there’s nothing but the rush of wind around the canopy. The aircraft glides on its long wings while the coasting propeller turns the motor into a generator, feeding about 9 kW back to the battery.

Then we turn to the east and slip into the landing queue behind a National Guard C-130 Hercules, and Caputo powers and slides the throttle forward. The motor springs to life again, pushing the airplane, and perhaps aviation itself, into the future.

This article was updated on 29 October 2026.

Tom Clynes, an IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, is a writer and photojournalist who covers science and the environment.

This sounds like a test plane more than a commercial one, but I guess that makes sense while companies are figuring out how to integrate new technologies into our existing safety regulations.The other thing that stands out to me is how the motors have redundant sub-systems. I can see the value, but it sure seems like a steep price to pay in terms of weight and complexity. Looking forward to seeing how that evolves.

#3225. Pangram’s new models spot AI fakes in images and video, it says

The AI text detection startup adds heatmaps, video uploads and browser alerts, but its accuracy figures are self-reported.

Pangram’s demo: a real photo of a restaurant whose wall mural is AI-generated (left), the Image 1.0 heatmap (centre) and the overlay (right).

Pangram launched Pangram Image 1.0 for AI images and the faster Image Flash 1.0 for video. It claims near-perfect scores on its own tests and 98.7% on the DF26 academic benchmark. Both are in its web app and API, and Image 1.0 is in its Chrome extension.

Pangram, a New York startup known for spotting AI-written text, has launched two models for detecting AI images and video, the company said on Wednesday. Pangram Image 1.0 checks still images, while the smaller, faster Pangram Image Flash 1.0 checks video frame by frame.

The image model can also draw a heatmap showing where AI content sits in a picture, such as a fake object added to a real photo. Pangram says it catches 99.2% of AI images and wrongly flags 0.27% of real ones.

In its own test, Pangram made AI copies of 100 real photos with 12 leading image generators, using prompts that closely matched each original. Image 1.0 scored 99.96% accuracy on that set. The test was designed by Pangram, not by outside reviewers.

For video, Pangram used DF26, an academic benchmark of 2,691 clips of people speaking to camera, published in September. Its authors found that both people and leading detectors did little better than chance at telling real clips from fakes.

Pangram says Flash 1.0 scores 98.7% on DF26, 29 points ahead of the next-best detector.

The new models also work on smaller images, down to 256 by 256 pixels from 512 by 512. Results below 512 pixels carry a lower-confidence warning. Pangram says it trains the models to see through compression, blur and noise, which platforms and people trying to fool detectors can add.

Image 1.0 now runs in Pangram’s Chrome extension, which flags AI content on social media, shopping and rental sites. Users can also upload videos in the web app, and the API now handles both images and video. Platforms are cracking down too: Snapchat has stopped recommending AI videos on Spotlight.

Pangram raised $9M in a round led by Menlo Ventures in July, when it first previewed image detection. Its text detector already runs on Substack.

AI detectors still make mistakes. In August, Pangram’s text tool flagged a Berkeley professor’s op-ed as partly AI-written, which she disputed.

Even Meta’s own image detector missed cropped fakes from its generator more than half the time in Reuters tests. On YouTube, a network that paid real actors to read AI scripts beat its detectors.

#3224. Palmer Square (PSBD) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

CLO debt reset cut financing costs while extending the reinvestment period.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Palmer Square Capital BDC Inc. (PSBD +0.91%) reported third quarter results focused on portfolio optimization and a disciplined capital allocation strategy through share repurchases. Management reported that the company executed a reset of its collateralized loan obligation debt, which reduced the weighted average cost of financing while extending the reinvestment period through 2031. The company prioritized share buybacks during the period, utilizing its expanded repurchase authorization to address the stock's discount to net asset value. Management stated that the investment strategy currently favors secondary market opportunities in broadly syndicated loans and direct private credit investments due to prevailing spread dynamics. The portfolio maintained a high concentration of senior secured positioning across diverse industries, with interest coverage ratios remaining stable despite heightened interest rate volatility.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Welcome to Palmer Square Capital BDC's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded. At this time, I'd like to turn the call over to Jeremy Goff, Managing Director. You may begin.

Jeremy Goff: Welcome to Palmer Square Capital BDC's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. Joining me this afternoon are Chris Long, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer; Matt Bloomfield, President; and Jeff Fox, Chief Financial Officer and Director. Palmer Square Capital BDC's Third Quarter 2026 financial results were released earlier today and can also be accessed on Palmer Square's Investor Relations website at palmersquarebdc.com. We have also arranged for a replay of today's event that can be accessed on our website. During this call, I want to remind you that the forward-looking statements we make are based on current expectations. The statements on this call that are not purely historical are forward-looking statements.

These forward-looking statements are not a guarantee of future performance and are subject to uncertainties and other factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed in the forward-looking statements, including and without limitation, market conditions caused by uncertainties surrounding interest rates, changing economic conditions and other factors we identified in our filings with the SEC. Although we believe that the assumptions on which these forward-looking statements are based are reasonable, any of those assumptions can prove to be inaccurate. And as a result, the forward-looking statements based on those assumptions can be incorrect. You should not place undue reliance on these forward-looking statements.

The forward-looking statements made during this call are made as of the date hereof, and Palmer Square Capital BDC assumes no obligation to update the forward-looking statements unless required by law. To obtain copies of SEC-related filings, please visit our website at palmersquarebdc.com. With that, I will now turn the call over to Chris Long.

Christopher Long: Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining us today for Palmer Square Capital BDC's Third Quarter 2026 Conference Call. On today's call, I will provide an overview of our third quarter results, touch on our market outlook, the current industry dynamics at play, and then turn the call to the team to discuss our portfolio activity and financial results. PSBD delivered solid financial performance in the third quarter, supported by a disciplined capital allocation strategy. We prioritized share repurchases during the quarter, buying back $5.2 million of PSBD shares under the expanded repurchase program that was announced last quarter.

This underscores our continued commitment to allocating capital in a way that prioritizes shareholder value while remaining selective in a moderate deal environment. During the third quarter, our team deployed $115 million of capital and generated total and net investment income of $26.6 million and $11.6 million, respectively. We delivered net investment income of $0.38 per share and paid a $0.38 per share total dividend, which includes a $0.02 supplemental distribution above our base dividend. Notably, our dividend payout represents an attractive 11.4% yield on NAV and 15.3% yield on the stock price as of October 30.

In further alignment with the priorities and approach I've just discussed, our Board has declared a fourth quarter base dividend of $0.36 per share with the supplemental dividend to be determined in the normal course. Turning to net asset value. Our NAV per share as of September 30, 2026, was $13.34, reflecting fair value adjustments resulting from pricing moves within the broadly syndicated loan market and an increase of $0.13 per share from the end of the second quarter. Matt will provide additional color on our broader outlook for credit and how it specifically relates to PSBD's portfolio momentarily.

But at a high level, we see a similar dynamic to what we discussed at the close of the second quarter, a multifaceted market environment that remains fluid. In the third quarter, specifically, we experienced heightened interest rate volatility late in the quarter with the 10-year Treasury yield recording one of its largest quarterly moves in history and the 30-year yield reaching multi-decade highs. Inflation remained persistent, prompting the Fed to act in September as economic data reinforced the need for a rate hike with the potential for additional increases in the months ahead. As I've shared in previous quarters, the Palmer Square platform was built for markets like these.

While the macro challenges we see today create a more complex investing environment, it is this kind of complexity that highlights the capabilities and experience of the platform behind PSBD and our ability to find opportunities and create shareholder value. As Matt will discuss, we continue to see and evaluate deals across our opportunity set in floating rate bank loans and private credit, which have continued to outperform traditional fixed income and corporate credit during the quarter. We believe the yields across the broader BDC sector, particularly given current discount to NAV, are becoming increasingly difficult for investors to ignore.

As we look at the opportunities set in front of us, we are further reassured by the resilience of corporate earnings and the relative stability of underlying credit performance, and are optimistic that attractive opportunities can arise even as deal activity remains muted by rate volatility and broader sentiment. Turning to AI and software for a moment. AI-related debt issuances continued to accelerate during the third quarter, competing with other income-generating products for investor capital. At the same time, we are closely monitoring growing opposition to data center permitting and construction, which could impact the pace of AI infrastructure development.

This remains an important trend to watch, particularly given that AI infrastructure investment represents a meaningful portion of GDP and corporate earnings growth trajectories. As we have previously discussed, we remain confident in our software portfolio, which is strategically focused on AI beneficiaries and management teams who have demonstrated an ability to adapt and innovate. As I conclude my remarks, I'd like to reiterate Palmer Square Capital Management's competitive advantage as one of the industry-leading global CLO managers.

The breadth of our platform, which provides extensive visibility across the entire broadly syndicated loan landscape, enables us to act selectively, and we believe the combined benefits to PSBD from our scale, long-standing relationships, and significant sourcing capabilities within the syndicated loan market continue to be underappreciated by the market. We remain focused on delivering the best possible outcomes for our portfolio and most importantly, our shareholders. We believe the flexibility of our liquid portfolio, combined with our active management approach and line of sight across the leveraged loan market positions us well to execute as market conditions evolve.

Looking ahead, if interest rate volatility and geopolitical uncertainty remain elevated, we expect it to continue weighing on deal activity in the fourth quarter. From our recent conversations with sponsors, we've heard anecdotally that transaction processes are taking longer to complete and deal time lines are increasingly being extended. That said, sponsors ultimately need to transact, and we expect activity to improve over time, although the pace of that improvement may be uneven. With that, I will hand the call over to Matt.

Matthew Bloomfield: Thank you, Chris. As Chris alluded to, credit performance remained consistent despite a volatile macro backdrop, which has been further compounded by inflationary pressures and the Fed increasing interest rates in September. Rising diesel prices resulting from ongoing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and Europe pose additional uncertainties related to the outlook for economic growth. Growing concerns about the costs of AI-related build-outs and the resulting impact rising AI debt levels have had on credit spreads has further added to recent credit volatility.

In light of these dynamics and consistent with our expectations through the summer, the BSL market saw relatively subdued but steady activity during the quarter, with a pickup in deal flow following Labor Day, followed by a notable pullback as we moved into the fourth quarter. As spreads remain tight, partly driven by market technicals, we saw several private credit borrowers refinance into the BSL market to take advantage of more attractive pricing. Encouragingly, we have also seen a modest pickup in sponsor-backed M&A activity across the software sector.

This momentum, coupled with multiple high-profile software refinancings, including Proofpoint, which priced in July, and Sophos, which priced in September, demonstrates the market's willingness to underwrite risk in the sector even as lenders remain increasingly risk-averse. As we have discussed in the past, for the right opportunities in the software sector, such as these in cybersecurity, we believe there will continue to be strong relative value and total return opportunities for those willing to do the work. During the quarter, we also observed that some lenders were able to secure more favorable terms, including stronger credit documentation, wider spreads, and in one instance, additional junior capital support, which we view as a constructive development for lenders. Turning to the portfolio.

We are pleased with performance during the third quarter, generating net investment income of $0.38 per share, $0.02 above our base dividend, along with modest NAV accretion compared to the second quarter. We also continue to focus efforts on optimizing the right side of the balance sheet, and were able to reduce leverage while simultaneously returning capital to our shareholders through our share repurchase program. These results reflect our active and disciplined approach to managing both our investments and balance sheet.

As discussed on our last earnings call, during the quarter, we reset and extended our BDC CLO, lowering the weighted average cost of debt to SOFR plus 1.39% from SOFR plus 1.72% while extending the reinvestment period to July 2031 and maturity to July 2039. Given the lower cost of financing through our CLO, we also reduced excess capacity under our Bank of America BSL funding facility to reduce associated unused fees. Together, these actions help enhance our funding efficiency and reduce carrying costs while preserving liquidity and financial flexibility should M&A activity accelerate. Notably, we reduced our leverage from 1.71x in the second quarter of 2026 to 1.63x in the third quarter of 2026.

This was driven by a combination of debt paydown and NAV appreciation during the quarter. We are pleased with the strength and flexibility of our balance sheet, which positions us to capitalize on attractive investment opportunities as they arise. Importantly, share repurchases remain a top near-term priority as we evaluate capital allocation opportunities against our broader investment mandate. Tactically, we currently see better relative value in private credit compared to the syndicated loan market given prevailing spread dynamics. And within the BSL market, we see more attractive risk-adjusted returns in the secondary market compared to new issuance. Our team continues to actively evaluate these opportunities and allocate where we see the most compelling value.

And while these are how we currently see the opportunity set, given the fluidity of the market, that can certainly change. Our investment portfolio as of September 30, 2026, had a fair value of approximately $1.09 billion, diversified across 45 industries that demonstrate strong credit quality, industry and company-specific tailwinds, and a variety of end markets. This compares to a fair value of $1.11 billion at the end of the second quarter of 2026, reflecting a decrease of approximately 2.3%. In the third quarter, we invested $115 million of capital, which included 31 new investment commitments at an average value of approximately $3.5 million. During the same period, we realized approximately $165.8 million through repayments and sales.

To recap key portfolio highlights, at the end of the third quarter, our weighted average total yield to maturity of debt and income-producing securities at fair value was 11.99% and our weighted average total yield to maturity of debt and income-producing securities at amortized cost was 8.38%. We believe our focus on first lien loans, combined with diversification across industries and company size contributes to a strong credit profile with exposure to 45 different industries. Further, our 10 largest investments account for just 10.92% of the overall portfolio, and our portfolio is 97% senior secured with an average hold size of approximately $4.1 million.

On a fair value weighted basis, our first lien borrowers have a weighted average EBITDA of $483 million, senior secured leverage of 5.71x, and interest coverage of 2.38x. Additionally, new private credit loans comprised 12.2% of overall new investments at a weighted average spread of 659 basis points over the reference rate. On a fair value basis, nonaccruals represent less than 1 basis point and on an at cost basis, only 96 basis points. Our PIK income represents approximately 2.18% of total investment income, well below our peers and the industry average. We've maintained an average internal rating of 3.6 on a fair value weighted basis for all loan investments.

Our rating is derived from a unique relative value-based scoring system. Stepping back, the line between syndicated and direct lending continues to blur with borrower relationships increasingly spanning both markets. We believe our ability to invest across these financing channels is a competitive advantage, allowing us to maintain and expand incumbent relationships while leveraging knowledge of these borrowers to identify attractive investment opportunities. At the same time, we remain disciplined in our approach to capital allocation, weighing new investments against other opportunities, including share repurchases with the goal of maximizing value for shareholders. As we close out the year, we remain confident in the credit performance of our portfolio and the sustainability of the base dividend heading into 2027.

We expect recent refinancing activity to be additive to earnings power and market implied base rate expectations to be supportive as well. Now I'd like to turn the call over to Jeff, who will review our third quarter 2026 financial results.

Jeffrey Fox: Thank you, Matt. Total investment income was $26.6 million for the third quarter of 2026, down 16.1% from the $31.7 million for the comparable prior year period. Income generation during the quarter reflected contractual interest income from our investments, which was impacted by lower base rates versus the prior year as well as a modest amount of paydown-related income and fee income. Total net expenses for the third quarter were $14.9 million compared to $18 million for the prior year period. Net investment income for the third quarter of 2026 was $11.6 million or $0.38 per share compared to $13.6 million or $0.43 per share for the comparable period last year.

During the third quarter of 2026, the company had a total net realized and unrealized gains of $2.4 million compared to total net realized and unrealized losses of $10.3 million in the third quarter of 2025. This consisted of net unrealized depreciation of $2.2 million related to existing portfolio investments and net unrealized appreciation of $9.2 million related to exited portfolio investments. At the end of the third quarter, NAV per share was $13.34, increasing from $13.21 at the end of the second quarter of 2026. Moving to our balance sheet. Total assets were $1.1 billion and total net assets were $403.4 million as of September 30, 2026.

At the end of the third quarter, our debt-to-equity ratio was 1.63x compared to 1.71x at the end of the second quarter of 2026. Available liquidity, consisting of cash and undrawn capacity on our credit facilities was approximately $195 million. This compares to approximately $331 million at the end of the second quarter of 2026. Finally, on November 4, the Board of Directors declared a fourth quarter 2026 base dividend of $0.36 per share, in line with our dividend policy. Furthermore, our policy continues to distribute excess earnings in the form of a quarterly supplemental distribution. And with that, I'd now like to open the call up for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from the line of Kenneth Lee with RBC Capital Markets.

Kenneth Lee: Just one on the liquid loan markets there. And you mentioned in the prepared remarks that you're preferring private credit versus the more liquid side right now. And you also mentioned that spreads remain tight. Just wondering if you could give a little bit more color in terms of some of the terms and documentation that you're seeing in the BSL markets right now.

Matthew Bloomfield: Ken, it's Matt. Thank you for the question. Yes, that's right. I mean, I think on the margin, we do see a little bit better relative value, particularly from a spread perspective on the private credit portion of the market. I think with some continued outflows in non-traded BDCs, that's led to, I'd say, modest spread widening in that market. And so net-net, we think there's continued to be some interesting opportunities there. Throughout most of the third quarter, spreads remained relatively tight on the broadly syndicated side of things, talking about kind of the primary market there, especially with some of the deal flow post Labor Day.

But certainly, what we've seen over the month of October with a lot of increased rate volatility in general, there's certainly some more, I'd say, interesting opportunities in the broadly syndicated secondary market, as we mentioned in the prepared remarks. To be quite frank, we haven't seen a whole host of kind of new issues coming to the market here recently as well. So I think net-net, from our vantage point, we think there'll be some better things to do on the secondary side of things versus primary. And as we move into early next year, that tends to be a slower quarter in general from M&A activity and deal flow.

But we'll have to see how things evolve over the next few months.

Kenneth Lee: Great. Very helpful there. And just one follow-up, if I may. You briefly referenced the dividend outlook there or at least the coverage. I wonder if you could just further expand upon that, thoughts on dividend coverage, especially given the current rate outlook and sort of the potential deal activity that you see coming up.

Matthew Bloomfield: Sure. Yes, I think as we kind of look forward and model out kind of where the portfolio sits today from a spread perspective, obviously, I alluded to my comments on some more attractive spreads on the private credit side and certainly have seen some spread widening across most credit markets, if not all credit markets in October. So I feel net-net better just about where spreads are at. Obviously, base rates, we saw an increase from the Fed in September. I think the market is trying to decide which way we're headed on a go-forward basis.

But certainly, there's been a little bit more rate hikes priced in throughout next year, which from our vantage point, we would certainly view as a bit of a tailwind for yields on the portfolio, all within the fact that borrowers are still in a very good shape from an interest coverage standpoint. We sit at 2.4x interest coverage across our portfolio. So we feel like there's a good cushion for those borrowers to absorb some more rate hikes without causing too much in the way of stress from a cash flow standpoint.

So all that put together, again, we feel pretty good about where we sit from a base dividend standpoint on the go forward and certainly anticipate paying out any of the additional excess income generated through the supplementals.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Melissa Wedel with UBS. Your next question comes from the line of Ethan Kaye with Lucid Capital Markets.

Ethan Kaye: Just wanted to ask about interest costs going forward. I know there were maybe some puts and takes here this quarter as it relates to kind of the CLO refinancing and the excess capacity removal. Can you talk about kind of like run rate if you expect this to be kind of a good run rate going forward, what we saw in 3Q here?

Matthew Bloomfield: Ethan, it's Matt. Thank you for that question. Yes, I think we feel pretty good about kind of where the right side of the balance sheet is now post the refinancing and extension on the CLO and the downsizing on the BofA facility. All of those are obviously floating rate based. So they'll kind of matriculate wherever base rates go. But from the spreads on those perspective, we feel really good about where those are at. We got very nice execution kind of took advantage of all the comments we've made over the past several quarters about spreads being tight across most credit markets.

And so we certainly look to take advantage of that in the third quarter as well by tightening those up. So I think on a go-forward basis, those should be pretty steady state, and we feel good for the kind of medium to longer term with those facilities in place.

Ethan Kaye: Great. And then I guess one more on the portfolio turnover looked a little bit higher this quarter, certainly relative to 1H and seemingly relative to kind of what some peers have shown so far this quarter. Anything that kind of drove the elevated exit levels?

Matthew Bloomfield: I think we -- as we looked across the portfolio during the quarter, we did see a fair amount of refinancing activity on the broadly syndicated side of things. As we alluded to in some prior calls, spreads remained pretty tight and in some cases, kept tightening throughout the quarter. And so we just thought from a relative value standpoint and a risk-adjusted return standpoint that we weren't necessarily being compensated for some of those. So we just took the paydowns in those cases. We also, as you'll probably see in the 10-Q, we sold a lot of our CLO mezz investments in the quarter.

Again, as we've talked about spreads being really tight across most credit markets, we just thought there'll be better opportunities from a capital deployment and from a spread perspective in other asset classes on a go-forward basis. So those are kind of the 2 I would highlight as being kind of ones to note in the quarter. But again, we also think we've got a lot of capacity now should volatility persist and more interesting opportunities arise on the secondary side of things on the syndicated loan side.

And certainly, as we've talked about in the prepared remarks, continue to think share repurchases make a lot of sense given where discounts are and where kind of the return on equity sits from those buybacks and debt paydown as well. We mentioned in the quarter, we paid down some of our debt facilities to continue to manage the overall leverage level. So those are all things that I think look pretty consistent as we sit here today in the fourth quarter.

Ethan Kaye: Great. And one more quick one, if I may. Noticed the weighted average maturity on new investment commitments this quarter looks significantly lower, significantly less than previous quarters. Does that have to do with kind of more secondary opportunities? Or I guess, what's driving that?

Matthew Bloomfield: Yes. Good catch and noted on that. I think the main thing we've seen there is we alluded to a couple of the refinancings that got done in the quarter. Most of those are -- some of those that we've seen and certainly ones that we participated in, in this quarter tended to be kind of 2- to 3-year extensions versus full 7-year refinancings. So that's part of it. I think those -- when it's a shorter wall, those tend to be more attractive in certain situations, not every situation. But for those select refinancings we participated in, that was a dynamic at play there.

And then yes, to your other comment, secondary transactions where we can find credits that we feel very comfortable in from a credit quality standpoint and a repayment perspective to the extent we can pick those up at discounts to par and those that have shorter maturity profiles. We think that kind of pull to par or the ability to get refinanced out at par on a shorter basis makes a lot of sense for the portfolio as well.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your next question comes from the line of Melissa Wedel with UBS.

Melissa Wedel: Hopefully, you can hear me this time.

Melissa Wedel: I wanted to touch on the repurchase activity. Can you remind us -- if I missed it, I apologize, remind us how much remaining capacity is on that plan?

Matthew Bloomfield: Yes. Of course, Melissa, this is Matt again. We have, as of the end of the third quarter, about $24.8 million left on that plan. So quite a bit of capacity left even after the $5.2 million this quarter.

Melissa Wedel: Got it. And then, of course, leverage did come down during the quarter and you had net exits. Just wondering how you're feeling about 1.63x at the end of the third quarter and how much room you think that -- how you balance the additional attractive potential repurchases you could continue to do going forward versus new capital deployment? And basically, should -- are you managing to maintain leverage at that level? Or how are you thinking about it?

Matthew Bloomfield: Yes. I mean, I think we talked last quarter, we were comfortable at the 1.71x. We certainly didn't want to go much higher than that. But given our ability to manage leverage from a debt paydown perspective, from the liquidity in our underlying portfolio, we felt really good about that. I'd say during the quarter, as we saw those opportunities come up that I just talked about on the prior question, we just didn't think it made sense to stay involved at some of those spread levels. So we took those paydowns, certainly paid down some debt with that.

As we sit here in the fourth quarter, we'll kind of make those same judgments if things aren't attractive from a relative value standpoint. We're happy to continue to take refinancings and deploy that into some debt paydown, into share buybacks. But as I noted, in October with some of the activity we've seen in the broader markets, on the margin, things are getting a little bit more interesting from a deployment standpoint. So we'll balance all of those things, but we feel good about where we sit from a leverage standpoint. Certainly, that can come down.

I don't know that we'll take it too much higher from an opportunity deployment set, but it's something that we feel very comfortable managing, and we'll just kind of see where the opportunity set lies as we move forward through the rest of this quarter and beyond.

Melissa Wedel: Got it. I think I'm at the end of the queue, so I'll ask one more. This was a good quarter also in terms of sort of stemming the outflows on NAV or the NAV depreciation and had not just stabilization but a slight uptick quarter-over-quarter. Can you talk about how you're thinking about NAV stability going forward because that's definitely an area we get questions about.

Matthew Bloomfield: Yes. I mean, I think it was kind of to unpack the third quarter on a monthly basis, I'd say July and August were pretty steady, kind of loan prices matriculated higher in general in the syndicated loan market as things were pretty stable. The back half of September got a little more volatile. As we just talked about, October in general was a pretty volatile market in credit at large, especially with everything going on in broader rates and inflation and whatnot. But we would ultimately like to see more stability across the markets. I think it's just good from a portfolio stabilization level.

I think we've obviously increased our private credit allocation over the past couple of years to roughly 15% of the portfolio now. So there are things I think we'd look to do to hopefully make things a little bit more stable. But as I mentioned, that volatility unlocks a lot of opportunities as well when you can execute in the secondary market at discounts to par. Over the long term, we think that should lead to accretiveness across the portfolio. And sometimes there's a little bit more volatility in the short term.

But when you see good credits that go from par and trade down a few points to the extent you can take advantage of that, we think that should build things back into the portfolio and lead to good returns on a go-forward basis, too. So that's kind of how we think about it. We're cognizant of it, but also with the liquid nature of our portfolio or at least the majority of the portfolio, that's something that's a little bit part of it, I suppose.

Operator: We have reached the end of our Q&A session. I will now turn the call back to Jeremy Goff, Managing Director, for closing remarks.

Jeremy Goff: Thank you, operator, and thank you all for your time today. We look forward to updating everyone on our fourth quarter and 2026 full year results in the new year. Have a great rest of your day.

Operator: This concludes today's call. Thank you for attending. You may now disconnect.

‘A Dog’s Perfect Christmas’ is cozy but no Christmas classic

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Netflix’s holiday movie slate for 2026 begins its rollout this week, starting with “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas,” a streaming original that so rigidly sticks to the genre conventions that it is as predictable as unwrapping a Christmas present from that one relative who always gets you an Axe body spray gift set. Within seconds, you know exactly what you’re getting.

All the trappings of a family-focused festive-themed comedy-drama are here. By the end, everything is wrapped up in a neat bow, all to send viewers into the credits with a warm fuzzy feeling. It’s a safe holiday movie created in a tinsel-laden laboratory, where artistic merit is not the end goal. Instead, the objective is to create a product palatable for all ages.

But if “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas” proves anything, it’s that throwing a couple of cute canine companions into the mix can make even a Christmas movie this flavorless at least tolerable. Which isn’t to say it has any original musings on the special connection between household pets and their owners. It doesn’t even break from the weary formula established in other dog movies like “A Dog’s Purpose” and “A Dog’s Journey.”

However, the dogs were lovable enough to thaw out even my cynical soul. It might not be a future Christmas classic — the likes of “It’s A Wonderful Life” and “Elf” will not fear their place in any family’s annual seasonal watchlist being pinched by this new Netflix movie — but dog lovers everywhere will probably find this film cozy enough to watch, if only once.

Based on the novel by W. Bruce Cameron, author of “A Dog’s Purpose,” this movie focuses on the Goss family. Their holiday festivities are already off to a rocky start, with grandpa Sander (Dennis Quaid) grieving the loss of his wife two years prior, husband Hunter (Milo Ventimiglia) putting work first, and mother Juliana (Kathleen Rose Perkins) struggling to find common ground with her moody teenage daughter, Ello (Brooke Lena Johnson).

Things take a further turn when a medical emergency throws the family into turmoil and threatens to bring a swift end to any lingering holiday cheer. It’s up to the Goss' wise old dog, a basset hound named Winstead (voiced by Thomas Haden Church), and an energetic new arrival, a Corgi puppy named Ruby (Sadie Hatch), to bring the humans back together.

I really cannot overstate just how generic “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas” is. All its narrative beats have been seen in countless other holiday movies, and it has no desire to rework the genre trappings. But whether you demand, or particularly look for, originality in your holiday watchlist is a matter of personal preference. If you want a cozy family comedy, it’s a suitable way to spend 100 minutes, and it'll probably make for great background noise while putting up your own seasonal decorations, if that's your thing.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

It’s been suggested that Netflix has a mandate that its movies need to reiterate key plot points for viewers only half-watching, and while the streamer denies this, 'A Dog’s Perfect Christmas' is evidence to the contrary.

Another notable area where “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas” comes up short is in its insistence on over-explaining. It’s been suggested that Netflix has a mandate that its movies need to reiterate key plot points for viewers only half-watching, and while the streamer denies this, “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas” is evidence to the contrary. Characters often speak unnaturally, regurgitating facts as if they know a third party is watching their holiday season unfold and might need a reminder (or three) to follow along.

But even if “A Dog’s Perfect Christmas” will no doubt be forgotten long before you take down your tree and household decorations for another year, in the moment, it’s by no means offensively bad. It’s just bland. But above all, the two dogs at the heart of the holiday crowd-pleaser are very cute and given enough screen time to make their presence felt.

“A Dog’s Perfect Christmas” celebrates family, especially these four-legged members of our homes who are just as important to the unit as any human. That’s a message that dog owners everywhere will relate to, and it gives this Netflix movie a crowd-pleasing quality. I guess it really does prove that the inclusion of a dog (or two) can make anything watchable.

Watch "A Dog's Perfect Christmas" on Netflix now

#3222. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s revamped StandBy to other iPhones

Apple released iOS 27.3 beta 1 today, with a surprisingly extensive set of new features and improvements across the system. One of them is the expansion of the iPhone Duo’s redesigned StandBy experience to other iPhone models. Here are the details.

When Apple announced the iPhone Duo, one of its exclusive new features was a redesigned StandBy experience with new clock faces and expanded customization options.

StandBy mode was introduced with iOS 17, and it essentially turns the iPhone into a smart display when placed horizontally while charging.

Until now, users of other iPhone models were limited to the original StandBy experience, which offered clock, widget, and photo views, but lacked the additional faces and more extensive customization options introduced with the iPhone Duo.

With iOS 27.3, however, Apple is extending the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces to other iPhones, with additional options for customizing their colors and complications. In addition to the new Calendar and Weather faces, the update adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face, letting users choose which shared photos appear in StandBy.

Users with an iPhone 11 or later can now also create multiple versions of the same StandBy face, each with its own customization options, and swipe between them.

iOS 27.3 is expected to launch in December. To learn more about StandBy and how to customize its different faces, follow this link.

#3221. ChatGPT can now make animated GIFs with OpenAI’s Images 2.6

Users can turn a prompt or photo into a GIF, then change its speed and edit single frames.

The ChatGPT app open on an iPhone, its dark start screen showing the OpenAI logo.

OpenAI is adding animated GIFs to ChatGPT with a new image model, Images 2.6. Users can make a GIF from text or a photo and edit its frames. Developers get two new API models, and OpenAI says people now make over 4 billion images a week.

OpenAI is rolling out animated GIFs in ChatGPT alongside a new image model, Images 2.6, The Verge reported on Wednesday. Users can turn a written prompt or an uploaded photo into a GIF.

Once a GIF is made, users can change how fast it plays, look at and edit single frames, and share it. Until now, ChatGPT could not make a GIF in one step. The feature arrives months after OpenAI shut down Sora, its AI video app, in March.

OpenAI says Images 2.6 also makes image generation in ChatGPT faster. It is rolling out to all ChatGPT and Codex users on the web, desktop and mobile.

Developers get two new API models: GPT-Image-2.6 Flare for speed and GPT-Image-2.6 Sunburst for quality. They follow the split OpenAI introduced with Images 2.5 in September, when Adobe put one of its models into Firefly.

Use keeps growing. OpenAI says people now make more than 4 billion images a week across ChatGPT and its API, up from 3 billion in September. The figures are OpenAI’s own and cover all image use, not only GIFs.

OpenAI has updated its image tools often this year. Images 2.0, launched in April, was its first image model that reasons before drawing. Last month, OpenAI began testing ads inside image generation in the US.

#3220. Xcode 27.3 adds GitHub Copilot to its built-in coding assistant

Apple released Xcode 27.3 beta 1 today with multiple new features, chief among them an expansion of its built-in coding assistant to support GitHub Copilot. Here are the details.

Since Xcode 26.3, developers have been able to integrate AI coding agents directly into Xcode, to help with tasks ranging from writing boilerplate code to updating entire projects based on their documentation, file structure, and more.

Apple initially introduced ChatGPT integration in Xcode 26, followed by Anthropic’s Claude. Then, in Xcode 26.3, the company expanded both integrations with agentic coding capabilities through OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Agent.

With Xcode 27, Apple added support for Google Gemini, alongside a redesigned interface, interactive planning, and multi-turn conversations.

Now, with Xcode 27.3, Apple is expanding the list of supported AI coding tools once again, this time adding GitHub Copilot.

The Xcode 27.3 beta 1 release notes include the following under the Coding Intelligence section:

As with the other agentic integrations, this is particularly good news for developers whose companies have standardized on GitHub Copilot, as they can now use their company’s preferred AI coding tool directly within Xcode.

Here are the full release notes for Xcode 27.3 beta 1:

Xcode 27.3 beta includes Swift 6.4 and SDKs for iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, tvOS 27.3, watchOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3. Xcode 27.3 beta supports on-device debugging in iOS 17 and later, tvOS 17 and later, watchOS 10 and later, and visionOS. Xcode 27.3 beta requires a Mac running macOS Tahoe 26.6 or later.

See Xcode Support to learn more about compatible platforms and deployment targets.

Xcode 27.3 is expected to be released in December, alongside macOS 27.3 and its counterparts.

To learn more about what’s coming to Xcode 27.3, follow this link.
