#3218. Systems Thinking Is Vital in the Age of AI

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Machines can automate drudgery but engineers make key decisions

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

Modern engineering projects increasingly combine human judgment with machine capability. An engineer can define a problem, then ask an artificial intelligence tool to search relevant research and technical standards, generate design options, test them in simulation, and compare the results. The engineer can then bring the results to specialists who understand the parts AI cannot judge on its own, such as whether a design can be built safely, whether it makes sense in a particular setting, or how it might affect its users. The final decision about whether and how to move forward remains a human responsibility.

AI can help engineers do early project steps that once required several people with different technical skills. The engineer’s role is therefore expanding from performing each technical step to deciding how people, machines, and specialists’ knowledge should work together on the project.

Engineering has always been divided into disciplines, and for good reasons. Electrical, mechanical, civil, software, and other engineering fields require deep knowledge that takes years to develop. AI does not replace that need. It simply changes how easily engineers can explore the parts of a problem that sit outside their own specialty.

Consider a software engineer working on a medical device. AI can help the engineer review relevant biomedical research, understand unfamiliar terms, analyze data, and build an early model.

That does not make the engineer a physician or biomedical expert. It allows the engineer to ask better questions before working with the experts.

The same is true in energy, transportation, manufacturing, and many other fields. A problem might begin as a software issue and then quickly involve hardware, safety measures, economics, human behavior, and regulations.

Engineers do not need to master every field; they need to recognize which expertise the problem requires and bring the right people and tools together.

Systems thinking thus becomes especially important. It requires looking at the whole problem: understanding how its parts affect one another, identifying constraints and failure points, and making trade-offs.

AI adds a new element to the process. Engineers must decide not only how the technical parts fit together but also what work to give to AI, what a person must check, when a specialist should make a decision, and when the problem needs to be redefined.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

This aspect is crucial because technical challenges in engineering are seldom static. As new insights emerge, objectives might shift, unseen limitations can surface, and the initial premise might prove flawed. Rather than rigidly following the starting specifications, an effective engineer adapts and refines the scope as a deeper understanding of the system develops.

Thus, engineering extends beyond mastering technical concepts; it is an adaptable, structured approach to navigating evolving challenges.

New evidence can change the goal, reveal a hidden constraint, or show that the original hypothesis was wrong. Effective engineers go beyond merely acting on the initial problem statement. They update it as the system becomes better understood.

In that sense, engineering is not only a body of technical knowledge, it is also a disciplined way of thinking about a project.

AI can produce convincing answers even when its assumptions are weak. It can generate code that works in one test but fails in another. It can summarize research without understanding which evidence is strongest, or optimize a design for the wrong goal. Such limits make human expertise more important, not less.

Machines are useful where speed, scale, search, pattern recognition, and data generation matter. People are essential where context, values, responsibility, and judgment matter. The challenge is to decide where each belongs.

An AI system might generate several designs for a medical sensor, for example, and predict how each will perform. An engineer can test the predictions and reject designs that violate technical requirements. A clinician can determine whether the sensor can be realistically used. Patients and practitioners might reveal problems that neither the engineer nor the developer considered. The final solution emerges from combining the perspectives.

The engineer is still a builder and specialist but increasingly also a coordinator of knowledge.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

The broader form of engineering creates an important role for IEEE. Its societies already bring together expertise in various technologies, engineering education, technical standards, and other fields. That makes IEEE well placed to help engineers work across specialties without weakening the value of specialization.

IEEE could create more communities organized around problems that require expertise from several fields. Examples include trustworthy clinical AI, resilient infrastructure, energy reliability, scientific discovery, and safe autonomous systems. An engineer could begin in a home discipline and then work with specialists from other IEEE communities as a project requires.

IEEE also can help set practical standards for human-machine collaboration. Engineers will need clear guidance on when AI-generated work must be checked, how uncertainty should be documented, when a specialist must make a decision, and who is responsible when a system uses both human judgment and machine output.

Those questions are becoming part of everyday engineering. They should not be left to each company or project manager to answer independently. A professional organization can provide common expectations that follow engineers as they move between jobs, industries, and technical fields.

AI does not make engineering disciplines less important; it makes the connections between them easier to use. Deep expertise gives engineers the foundation to judge what is sound. Systems thinking helps them understand how different parts of a problem fit together. AI can extend engineers’ ability to explore, test, and communicate across fields. Human judgment gives the work direction and responsibility.

An engineer is not defined only by a job title or a fixed set of tasks. An engineer is someone trained to understand complex systems, define and redefine problems, bring together the knowledge and tools needed to solve them, test whether solutions work, and take responsibility for the outcome.

That is what it means to be an “unbound” engineer.

The boundaries between specialties become easier to cross, and machines might take on more of the technical work, but the core of engineering remains human: deciding what problem is worth solving, what evidence is good enough, how the pieces fit together, and what to do when the answer is uncertain.

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

#3216. Why Alphabet Stock Popped on Wednesday

A Democratic sweep might be just the medicine Google needs to prosper.

Shares of Alphabet (GOOGL +3.18%) (GOOG +3.25%) charged higher Wednesday, gaining as much as 5.9%. By the time trading closed, the stock was still up 3.2%.

The catalyst that sent the artificial intelligence (AI) and cloud provider higher was the results of the U.S. election.

Democrats took control of both the House and the Senate, and won several high-profile gubernatorial races. One of the rallying cries among the party faithful was stricter oversight and regulation of data centers, which have become a hot-button issue for some voters. Indeed, following months of public outcry, there were an estimated 50 ballot measures across the country focused on data centers, with many seeking moratoriums and strict accountability for the use of local resources.

Texas, for example, is one of the biggest destinations for data centers over the next couple of years, accounting for 41% of all capacity scheduled to come online in 2028. However, Democrat governor-elect Gina Hinojosa courted voters with the promise of a moratorium on data centers in the state until the legislature examines the effects of these facilities on electricity consumption and prices, water use and availability, and air quality, among other factors.

Texas isn't the only state taking a close look at the impact of data centers. Ohio, Georgia, and Arizona are lined up behind the Lone Star State in terms of data center construction projects, and all three just elected Democrats to the governor's office.

Alphabet has leaned into its cloud and AI services, with significant capital expenditures (capex) to support rising demand. In Q3, Google Cloud revenue soared 103% year over year to $30.7 billion, driven by demand for AI.

Unfortunately, investors focused on Alphabet's negative free cash flow of $9 billion and plans for roughly $200 billion in capex spending in 2026, up from $90 billion last year. This sent the stock down 13% on the day following its report-- the largest single-day decline in Alphabet’s history.

The good news is that any moratorium will likely hurt competition and benefit hyperscalers like Google, which already has a network of data centers. It would also slow the company's capex spending, which would boost profits and cash flow along the way.

And at just 15 times earnings -- near last week's all-time low -- Alphabet stock represents a compelling opportunity for discerning investors.

Danny Vena, CPA has positions in Alphabet. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Alphabet. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3215. Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Nearly 70 percent of respondents say they want an AI assistant in their next device, according to a new report

Qualcomm builds intelligent, connected, computing and AI solutions that transform industries and advance human progress.

A recent report by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide, shows that around 70 percent of respondents express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.

This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies.

For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules?

It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user.

These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want?

A Personal AI report, commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments.

The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI.

Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor.

Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction.

With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report.

The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit.

The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users:

But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI.

Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix.

The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories.

Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch.

Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time.

Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents.

Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf.

Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear.

All percentages, consumer behaviors, and attitudes stated in this report are based only on the responses of the individuals who participated in our survey.

Qualcomm Technologies is a global leader in communications and computing technologies, including leading-edge AI, high-performance, low-power computing, and connectivity solutions. Headquartered in San Diego, Calif., the company develops technologies for next-generation mobile networks and smart devices, and designs semiconductors such as mobile processors and AI chips.

#3214. Apple cuts engineers’ daily AI budgets as it reins in spending

Some engineers' daily cap fell from $300 to $200, and some other teams could drop to $25.

The Apple logo on the lid of a silver MacBook Pro.

Apple cut the daily AI spending cap for some engineers from $300 to $200 last month and plans further cuts, Bloomberg reports. It comes as CEO John Ternus pushes for a leaner Apple, while the company’s R&D costs rose 32% on AI and infrastructure.

Apple has cut how much some engineers can spend on AI models each day, from $300 to $200, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with the change. It plans more cuts that could take some engineering teams down to $100 a day.

Many staff outside engineering already have a $100 daily cap, and Apple has considered lowering that to $25 for some teams. Employees who need more can ask senior leaders for an exemption. Apple declined to comment.

The budgets cover tokens, the units of data that AI models process. Writing and debugging code can use a lot of them. Apple staff can use Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini, and some teams are being told to switch to cheaper models or ones that run on the device.

Reactions inside Apple are mixed, according to Bloomberg. Some staff say few people used their full $300 allowance. Others see the cuts as a sign of wider cost cutting and worry about layoffs, after Apple cut over 200 jobs in August.

Since becoming chief executive on 1 September, John Ternus has pushed Apple to run faster and leaner, and has cut layers of management. Some divisions have also hired outside consultants to review how efficiently they work.

Apple’s overall spending is still rising. Research and development costs rose 32% in its 2026 fiscal year on higher infrastructure and AI costs, the company said in its annual report this week. Operating expenses rose 22% to $75.5B.

Apple is not alone. Microsoft set division-level AI budgets in July, Tesla caps staff at $200 a week and Uber limits each AI coding tool to $1,500 a month. Accenture has gone further, capping Claude at $29 a month.

Across the industry, firms are capping staff AI use as their bills grow.

A drone landing pad is very useful if you're taking off from a rocky or sandy surface. The FPVtosky Nighttime Reflective Drone Landing Pad is waterproof and easy to clean, and it's portable and easy to carry. It's reflective which makes it easier to land your drone when visibility is low.

The Anker Prime 27,650mAh 3-Port 250W is extremely portable and lightweight, and it can quickly charge large devices, such as MacBooks and drones, with its 250W power delivery. It also features three ports to charge multiple devices simultaneously.

The Fujifilm Instax mini 13 takes lovely photos with retro colors, and its controls are so straightforward that anyone, regardless of age or experience, can use it. It comes in fun colors, and it’s great value for money. It's the perfect gift for those who enjoy physical prints. I awarded it 4.5-stars in my Instax mini 13 review.

If your loved one doesn't need an instant camera but likes physical prints, the Fujifilm Instax mini Link 3 Printer makes for a thoughtful gift. It uses Bluetooth to connect with and directly print from your smartphone, and you can use its companion app to create collages, too.

There's no such thing as "too much film," and if you ask any instant photographer, they'll say that film's getting too expensive — so why not gift your loved one this lovely Fujifilm Instax mini Pastel Galaxy film pack? The film has a wonderful starry border, so it's great for space fans.

Okay, you've got your loved one a film pack and an instant camera, now get them an Instax mini Photo Album with 112 pockets so they have somewhere to store them. I love flipping through my family's photo albums whenever I visit them, so this is a great choice for fans of physical prints.

Imagine going to a bar with your friends and pulling out a Mini Photo Album to show everyone. Now that's cool. This one from Fintie features 52 pockets and comes in lovely colors, suitable for every mood or type of photographer.

If you or your loved one want to display your instant prints around your house, now you can. The Orga'Neat Picture Holder is spacious enough to hold a 2x3-inch mini print, and it has a see-through case so everyone can admire the time you went skydiving in the Maldives.

While the aforementioned accessories make great gifts for Fujifilm Instax shooters, this Polaroid Large Photo Album is for, well, Polaroid snappers. It can store up to 160 photos and is made of cardboard so it looks classy. It's designed for Polaroid i-Type, 600 and SX-70 film, so make sure you find out what camera it is your loved one owns before you buy it.

The Polaroid Now and Now+ Filter Set is perfect for those who own either of those cameras. There are five creative filters in the box, including starburst, red vignette, orange, blue and yellow, and these can help photographers get creative with their shots.

If you've got a teen in your life, and they love LED lamps and instant cameras, you can combine their adoration for both with this 50 LED 5m Photo Clips String Lights set. It's battery powered and comes with a remote that lets you swap between different lighting modes.

Who says your furry friend can't join in on the holiday fun? This Dog Harness GoPro Mount is ideal for those with dogs (or cats, even) and a GoPro action camera. Your pet can wear it and then record the world from their POV. Trust me, it'll make for very cute videos.

The TELESIN Waterproof Case is an anti-fog underwater housing cage for the DJI Osmo Action line-up. It can protect your camera as you record underwater activity deep to 60 meters or 196 feet without worrying about leaks. It's also sturdy enough to protect your camera lens and screen against high impact drops, dents and scratches.

SanDisk's 256GB Extreme microSDXC UHS-I microSD card boasts not just massive storage space, but also fast read (190mbps) and write speeds (130mbps). Offload speeds also top at 190mbps so you can quickly transfer content between devices, making it the ideal microSD card for 4K and 5K UHD capture.

If you know someone that owns a 360° camera, like the Insta360 X6, then an invisible selfie stick is a fantastic gift, allowing them to capture footage from an overhead point of view with no selfie stick — it’s as if the camera is floating above them and looks very surreal, but very cool.

#3211. When Electric Cars Were for Women

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

#3210. Prediction: This Is How Much IonQ Stock Will Be Worth by the End of 2027

IonQ's stock has had a rough year, but a turnaround could be coming.

Quantum computing is heating up, and there could be some breakthroughs over the next few years. IonQ (IONQ -1.50%) is one of the leaders in this space and is generating pretty sizable revenue figures for still being in a start-up stage. However, it remains to be seen whether it's a viable investment, as IonQ hasn't released any commercially viable equipment and is relying on partnerships and outside funding to keep its business going.

2027 could be a huge year for the company, as it has a major product launch coming that could dramatically accelerate its business trajectory. That could lead to huge upside for the beaten-down stock, potentially being worth $80 by the end of 2027 -- over a double from today's levels.

Next year, IonQ's 256-qubit system is expected to launch and utilize the same technology that set the world record for quantum computing accuracy. This is a big deal, as the two hurdles any quantum computing competitor must clear are accuracy and size.

Quantum computing can be done right now; the question is whether you can trust the results. Some of the best companies in this industry are struggling to achieve 99.9% 2-qubit fidelity, which means that the quantum computer will make an error after passing through two operations one time out of every 1,000 operations. That's a major problem, and with complex calculations, it could lead to a computing error effect. IonQ's technology has achieved 99.99% fidelity. While that extra 0.09% may not sound like a lot, that pushes the threshold to one error in every 10,000 operations. IonQ's accuracy is better than everyone else's because it uses a different quantum computing technique, known as trapped-ion quantum computing. This pathway trades off computing speed for accuracy, and that could give IonQ a leg up on every competitor, especially in the early stages of quantum computing.

Next up is size. Companies have struggled to make scalable quantum computers that can handle commercial-level problems. IonQ is taking the next step by launching its 256-qubit computer in early 2027, for which it already has several preorders. This will be an innovative system and could even provide some commercial viability. However, IonQ has repeatedly stated that it believes a 10,000-qubit computer will be necessary to achieve commercial viability. IonQ has a road map to building its 10,000-qubit computer, which it believes will be fault-tolerant, leading to nearly perfect accuracy.

If IonQ can achieve this, the sky is the limit for the stock, as it will easily be one of the top players in this space. But what would a short-term investment look like by the end of next year?

Because IonQ isn't really a viable business right now and is a more speculative investment, its stock rises and falls with the risk tolerance of the market. The market is currently in a risk-off state, and quantum computing stocks have really struggled. IonQ is no exception, down about 65% from its all-time high set in October 2025.

However, IonQ's business has grown, and the stock isn't as expensive as it once was (though it's still pricey). When next year's projections are priced in, it doesn't look so bad.

I wouldn't be surprised to see IonQ regain its old swagger if the launch of its 256-qubit system is successful. I think that could send the stock back to all-time-high levels of over $80 per share, which would be a sizable gain from today's $30 levels. As a result, the stock looks like a buy here.

Keithen Drury has positions in IonQ. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends IonQ. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3209. Apple now explicitly bans employees from using confidential information in prediction markets

Apple has updated its insider trading policy to explicitly prohibit employees from using confidential information to bet on prediction markets. Here are the details.

Following yesterday’s fiscal Q4 2026 earnings report, Apple today published its fiscal 2026 Form 10-K, which is a mandatory annual filing with the SEC that provides a detailed look at the company’s finances, business, and risks.

Among the documents included in the filing is an updated version of Apple’s insider trading policy.

Until last year, Apple’s insider trading policy, filed with the SEC as Exhibit 19.1, included the following prohibitions:

However, the updated policy includes a new prohibition:

No Trading in Prediction Markets Based on Confidential Information. Do not participate in “prediction markets” or similar platforms to wager, bet, trade, buy or sell contracts based on the outcome of future events, or otherwise enter into event contracts, when such activity involves the use of Apple Confidential Information (as defined in Apple’s Business Conduct Policy) about Apple or any other company (including Apple suppliers, manufacturers, vendors or customers, such as cellular network carriers or other business partners) obtained in connection with your work at Apple. You must also not tip Apple Confidential Information to others who may participate in such markets. Apple Confidential Information includes, but is not limited to, material nonpublic information. This prohibition applies whether or not the activity constitutes insider trading or securities trading under applicable laws.

While much of this may seem obvious, how insider trading rules apply to prediction markets has been something of a gray area, to put it mildly. And while major prediciton markets explicitly ban the practice in their terms of service, enforcement remains a challenge.

In Apple’s case, the new language explicitly extends restrictions beyond traditional securities trading, making it clear that employees cannot use confidential information to place bets on prediction markets, even when those transactions don’t qualify as insider trading under applicable laws.

You can read Apple’s full 2026 Form 10-K on its Investor Relations page.

#3207. Stop teaching leadership. Start letting people practise it

Managers raised on interactive games are still trained through slides and scripted workshops. Immersive simulations let them practise conflict, judgement and difficult conversations before real teams pay the price.

Organizations are preparing a generation raised on digital technology and interactive games to lead in a world of complexity. Yet many still train managers through presentations and scripted workshops. This is a costly mistake. If we want leaders who can navigate conflict, uncertainty, and human behavior, we must stop telling them how to lead.

We must give them opportunities to practise it.

I have spent decades exploring how emotional intelligence works in real situations. I believe leadership development is failing to keep pace with the people it needs to develop.

Emerging managers are accustomed to exploring possibilities and testing decisions. They are used to learning from failure and adapting when circumstances change. Yet traditional training too often delivers predetermined answers. It measures success by attendance or course completion. Real workplaces demand something far more challenging.

This is not about adding points, badges, or competitions to existing courses. Gamification adds game-like rewards to an activity. Immersive learning goes further. It uses interactive scenarios, role-play, meaningful objectives, and decisions with consequences to develop practical skills.

A corporate target becomes a quest. A key performance indicator becomes a challenge. It requires people to allocate resources, collaborate, assess incomplete information, and change direction when their first attempt fails.

Consider a character whose special power is generating fire. Used carefully, it can solve a problem. Used recklessly, it destroys everything around it, including the people the character needs. Leadership strengths work the same way.

Confidence becomes arrogance when unchecked. Analytical thinking becomes paralysis when taken too far. Empathy becomes avoidance when it prevents difficult conversations. Immersive scenarios allow people to discover these consequences before their behavior damages a real team.

The need is becoming more urgent as AI transforms work. Harvard Business Impact’s 2026 Global Leadership Study found that 53% of respondents expected leaders to make greater use of AI in strategic decision-making this year. As these tools become more influential, leaders must become better at exercising judgment, understanding people, and taking responsibility for decisions.

AI can analyze data and recommend actions. It cannot replace the human responsibility to understand how those actions affect others.

This approach has an academic foundation. A 2026 study published in the International Journal of Serious Games examined a live role-play simulation designed for school leaders. Feedback from 72 principals and vice principals highlighted opportunities to explore evidence-informed decisions through complex scenarios, feedback, and reflection. The findings support taking immersive learning seriously as a tool for leadership development.

Researchers studying role-playing also use the term “bleed”. It describes how emotions, attitudes, and aspects of identity can spill over between a character and the person playing it. A 2024 paper published in the International Journal of Role-Playing offers a useful perspective on workplace learning. It explored how these experiences can influence a player’s sense of self.

Practicing assertiveness in a simulated conversation, for example, may help someone feel more prepared to speak up in a difficult meeting. Whether that confidence carries into the workplace depends on the individual and the learning environment. It also depends on opportunities to apply and reflect on the experience.

Organizations that ignore this opportunity risk producing managers who can recite leadership principles but struggle when relationships become difficult. As AI takes on more routine work, these workplaces could become increasingly automated, impersonal, and disconnected from the people they serve.

Organizations that embrace immersive development can create opportunities for teams to practise adaptability, collaboration, and creative problem-solving. Teams can also learn to value different personalities and cultural perspectives.

I am in my late 60s. I believe experienced leaders have a responsibility to listen to younger managers rather than dismiss how they learn. If you lead an organization, stop treating immersive development as an optional experiment. Replace one conventional training session with a realistic simulation.

Give participants conflicting priorities, limited information, and a difficult conversation to navigate. Let them try, fail, reflect, and try again. Then assess whether their behavior changes at work.

We do not need to abandon established leadership principles. We need to stop teaching them in ways that leave people unprepared to use them. The future is human. As AI advances, our success will depend on empathy, emotional awareness, sound judgment, and meaningful interaction.

The organizations that thrive will be those that teach people not simply to perform like machines, but to lead like humans.

Dr. Robin Hills is a specialist in emotional intelligence and the director of Ei4Change, an emotional intelligence learning and development (show all) Dr. Robin Hills is a specialist in emotional intelligence and the director of Ei4Change, an emotional intelligence learning and development organization based in Greater Manchester, United Kingdom. His work draws on decades of applied business experience and research-informed approaches to psychology, neuroscience, and positive psychology. He focuses on helping individuals and organizations translate emotional intelligence into practical skills for leadership, communication, decision-making, resilience, and collaboration in a changing world for professionals and teams.

#3206. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3205. macOS 27.3 adds native Markdown rendering to Quick Look

Starting with macOS 27.3, users can preview Markdown files with proper formatting directly in Quick Look. Here are the details.

Apple released macOS 27.3 beta 1 today, with new Safari features, including Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode, expanded Siri AI capabilities, and new tools for third-party developers.

Among the smaller changes coming to the Mac is a welcome improvement to Quick Look. As of macOS 27.3 beta 1, .md files are rendered with proper formatting directly in Quick Look, rather than displaying their raw Markdown syntax.

Apple has been expanding Markdown support across its platforms, including the ability to import and export Markdown files in Notes. Markdown has also become increasingly important with the rise of AI agents, which use .md files to store instructions, context, and other information.

In fact, as Federico Viticci noted today on X, Apple’s new Siri AI app skills feature also uses Markdown-based SKILL.md files, allowing developers to provide instructions that help Siri perform complex tasks within their apps.

What a journey for Markdown, @gruber The new Siri AI developer framework now officially uses skills, with specific Markdown guidance for SKILL .md agent files https://t.co/koi8K541le pic.twitter.com/TF72JJZRXc

For the uninitiated, Markdown is a simple text formatting syntax created by John Gruber in 2004, and has since become widely used for writing documentation, publishing content online (including this very post), and, more recently, providing instructions to AI agents.

Markdown is a text-to-HTML conversion tool for web writers. Markdown allows you to write using an easy-to-read, easy-to-write plain text format, then convert it to structurally valid HTML.

In practice, this means you can create headings, bold text, lists, and links using just a few simple characters. And, starting with macOS 27.3, you’ll be able to preview the results directly in Quick Look, without having to open the file in a separate app.

#3199. XPEL: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Dealer channel relief and a China plant feeding non-U.S. markets could reshape XPEL's margins, but both depend on a 2027 rollout.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 4, 2026, XPEL (XPEL -0.85%) reported revenue growth of 9.9% to $137.8 million alongside expanding gross margins. The automotive protective film maker faces short-term regulatory friction in U.S. auto dealerships, but it's scaling direct international distribution and expanding domestic manufacturing to drive long-term operating leverage (growing revenue faster than operating expenses).

Three key takeaways from management's comments stand out for long-term investors.

Federal scrutiny and state regulations targeting undisclosed vehicle add-ons created uncertainty for dealership partners, causing sales through that channel to flatten. Management expects fourth-quarter performance to mark the trough as dealers update sales software and offer protective films as optional accessories rather than preinstalled packages.

XPEL is transitioning to direct distribution and in-house manufacturing, expanding its footprint through a new plant in Texas and an acquired facility in China. Supplying non-U.S. markets from the Chinese facility in early 2027 will lower production costs and expand gross margin (the percentage of revenue remaining after direct cost of goods sold).

Opportunities with original equipment manufacturers (OEMs, vehicle makers) have expanded rapidly, with a project pipeline double the company's historical total. The acquisition of the graphics supplier VISCO adds vehicle personalization capabilities and opens access to new auto manufacturer accounts.

Short-term headwinds in the Middle East create friction, yet operational progress stays on track. Internal manufacturing investments in Texas remain scheduled for a mid-2027 launch, supporting long-term operating margin goals while disciplined overhead cost control provides steady efficiency.

With regulatory resets nearing completion and direct international operations scaling up, execution across key markets positions the business for broader momentum.

#3196. Android 17 adoption hits a staggering 1% – why you really should update now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

Only a quarter of Android phones have even made it to Android 16.

Android 17 adoption hasn’t been speedy. According to the most recent data from heise.de via Android Studio, as reported by Android Authority, Android 17 has reached just 1% of active devices since its release in June 2026.

While Android 16 is finally the most used Google OS for Android devices, at 25.4% of active Android devices, these distribution figures indicate that getting users to upgrade to even newer software is an uphill battle.

It’s true that Android 17 has had less time to reach devices than Android 16 did when the previous distribution snapshot was published, but the minuscule adoption rate underscores how slowly the latest release is infiltrating the Android ecosystem.

Also: How Android 17 stops network snoops and SMS blasters now

Plus, the data show that more Android users than not are running versions that are many years old. I’m all for not fixing what’s not broken, but when Android 14 is the second most widely used version (15.% of devices are still running it), while Android 15 trails not far behind at 14.7%, there’s a pretty large chunk of individuals who may be putting themselves (and their data) at risk.

And it doesn’t end there. Android 13 and Android 11 are still on the table for 11.8% and 10.1% of users, with almost another 10% still using Android 12. That’s about another 30% of users still running Android 13 or older.

Though the numbers indicate that almost 60% of active Android devices are running Android 14 or newer, about 40% of users haven’t even upgraded to Android 14 or later.

Also: This Android 17 setting logs suspicious activity on your phone for troubleshooting

While the numbers are staggering, they’re not surprising. Android updates typically lag behind iOS updates. While the iPhone and its software are both designed, controlled, and distributed by Apple, Android updates must roll out from a single starting point to a wider array of mobile devices and systems to reach users. While Google is responsible for the core of the Android system, those updates must then be curated, reviewed, and pushed to every device that uses Android. This includes phones from Google, Samsung, Nothing, and more, which usually requires adaptations from each manufacturer. Apple’s updates are often adopted faster because there’s no middle entity between iOS and the user, while Android’s process is rather fragmented.

Keep in mind that Google no longer publishes a regularly updated public distribution chart, so this data isn’t from a real-time survey of every Android device. There’s only cumulative adoption data through Android Studio, and these estimates are derived from those figures and cover devices that contacted the Google Play Store during a seven-day period.

It’s always good practice to keep your device updated to the latest available software that your system allows. There are a few great reasons why those eligible for Android 17 should upgrade, including improved features — like the ability to “bubble” apps and stop network snoops and SMS blasters.

Also: I enabled Android’s new security feature that detects fake cell towers – here’s why

Plus, it’s the most proactive thing you can do for your device. Software updates usually include improvements to your phone’s operation, speed, security, and more, and it’s an easy (and free) way to keep your phone healthy.
